Jack polynomials and some identities for partitions

Michel Lassalle
Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique
Institut Gaspard Monge, Université de Marne-la-Vallée
77454 Marne-la-Vallée Cedex, France
lassalle @ univ-mlv.fr
http://igm.univ-mlv.fr/~lassalle/index.html

Mathematics Subject Classification 2000 : 05A10, 05A17, 05E05, 33C52, 33C80
partitions, (shifted) symmetric functions, (shifted) Jack polynomials, transition probabilities.

Introduction

A partition $\lambda= (\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n)$ is a finite weakly decreasing sequence of positive integers, called parts. The number $n=l(\lambda)$ of parts is called the length of $\lambda$, and $|\lambda| = \sum_{i = 1}^{n} \lambda_i$ the weight of $\lambda$. For any $i\geq1$, $m_i(\lambda) = \textrm{card} \{j: \lambda_j = i\}$ is the multiplicity of $i$ in $\lambda$. Clearly one has $l(\lambda)=\sum_{i} m_i(\lambda)$ and $|\lambda|=\sum_{i} i m_i (\lambda)$. We identify $\lambda$ with its Ferrers diagram $\{ (i,j) : 1 \le i \le l(\lambda), 1 \le j \le \lambda_i \}$ and set $$z_\lambda= \prod_{i\ge1} {i}^{m_i(\lambda)} m_i(\lambda)!.$$

In this paper we consider the problem of evaluating sums of the following type $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_\mu}\prod_{k \ge 1} (S_k)^{m_k(\mu)},$$ where $S_k$ is a formal series, depending on some indeterminates. The more elementary sum of this kind is well known. Let $X$ be an indeterminate and $n$ a positive integer. We write $$(X)_n = X(X+1) \ldots (X+n-1) \quad,\quad [X]_n = X(X-1) \ldots (X-n+1)$$ for the raising and lowering factorials and $\binom{X}{n} = [X]_n/n!$. Choosing $S_k=X$, one has $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{X^{l(\mu)}}{z_\mu} = \binom{X + n - 1}{n} = \frac{(X)_{n}}{n!}.$$

Let $X_{0}$ and $X=(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots)$ be (infinitely many) independent indeterminates. In we considered another summation of the same type $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_\mu}\prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(\sum_{r \ge 0}u^r\frac{(k)_r}{r!} X_r \right)}^{m_k(\mu)}$$ and gave its formal series expansion.

In this paper we investigate a natural generalization of our previous result and give the formal series expansion of $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(\sum_{r,s \ge o} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\,\frac{(k)_s}{s!}\, X_{r+s}\right)}^{m_{k}(\mu)}.$$

The interest of this result is twofold. Firstly it involves new combinatorial objects whose background remains quite mysterious. Actually the given explicit expansion is written in terms of a new family of coefficients associated to partitions, which are themselves built in terms of another new family of positive integers. Both objects generalize classical binomial coefficients, but it should be emphasized that their combinatorial interpretation remains very obscure. It is an intriguing problem to clarify this underlying structure, which would at the same time provide a bijective proof of our result.

Secondly any specialization of the indeterminates $X_i$ may lead to a different application of our formula. Here our attention keeps mainly focused on symmetric function theory and (shifted) Jack polynomials.

Let $\alpha$ be some positive real number, $\lambda$ a partition and $A_\lambda$ the family of its so called “$\alpha$-contents” $\{j-1-(i-1)/\alpha, (i,j) \in \lambda\}$. Specializing $X_i$ to the $i$th power sum symmetric function $p_i$ evaluated on $A_\lambda$, we obtain the series expansion of $$\frac{(x+y+1)_{\lambda}}{(x+y)_{\lambda}}\, \frac{(x)_{\lambda}}{(x+1)_{\lambda}},$$ where $x,y$ are two indeterminates, and $(x)_\lambda$ is some natural generalization of the classical raising factorial.

It turns out that two families of shifted symmetric functions, closely related to (shifted) Jack polynomials, have a generating function of this type. Our formula provides an explicit expression for these shifted symmetric functions, thus proving (and improving) some earlier conjectures. These expressions are new even in the case $\alpha=1$, which corresponds to (shifted) Schur functions.

Our results have some connection with the works of Kerov. To any Young diagram are associated two discrete probability distributions, generalizing the Plancherel transition and co-transition classical probabilities. It turns out that the two shifted symmetric functions explicited here are the moments of the $\alpha$-content random variable with respect to these distributions.

Another consequence of our results is to allow a very easy computation of the expansion of Jack polynomials in terms of power sum symmetric functions. We hope to report about this application in a forthcoming paper.

Combinatorial tools

Positive integers

We first recall some results about a new family of positive integers, which we have introduced in.

Let $n,p,k$ be three integers with $1 \le k \le n$ and $0 \le p \le n$. We define $${\binom{n}{p}}_{k} = \frac{n}{k} \ \sum_{r \ge 0} \binom{p}{r}\binom{n-p}{r} \binom{n-r-1}{k-r-1}.$$ We have obviously $${\binom{n}{p}}_{k} = 0 \quad \textrm{for} \quad k>n \quad, \quad {\binom{n}{p}}_{1}=n \quad, \quad {\binom{n}{p}}_{k} ={\binom{n}{n-p}}_{k}.$$ These numbers generalize the classical binomial coefficients, since we have $${\binom{n}{0}}_{k} = \binom{n}{k} \quad,\quad {\binom{n}{1}}_{k}=k \binom{n}{k} \quad,\quad {\binom{n}{p}}_{n} = \binom{n}{p},$$ the last property being a direct consequence of the classical Chu-Vandermonde formula.

Other special values have been computed in, where it was also shown that the numbers ${\binom{n}{p}}_{k}$ are positive integers. A combinatorial interpretation of these numbers has been given in.

In we gave the following generating function $$\sum_{k= 1}^n {\binom{n}{p}}_{k} {\left(\frac{z}{1-z}\right)}^k = n z \;{}_2F_1\!\left[ \begin{matrix}p+1,n-p+1\\ 2\end{matrix};z\right],$$ where as usual the classical Gauss hypergeometric function is denoted by $${}_2F_1\!\left[\begin{matrix}a,b\\ c\end{matrix};z\right]= \sum _{i \ge 0}\frac {(a)_i(b)_i} {(c)_i}\;\frac{z^i}{i!}.$$ In other words the generating function $$G_n(y,z) =\sum_{p=0}^{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} {\binom{n}{p}}_{k} y^p {\left(\frac{z}{1-z}\right)}^k$$ can be written $$G_n(y,z) = n z \sum_{p=0}^n y^p \,{}_2F_1\!\left[\begin{matrix}p+1,n-p+1\\ 2\end{matrix};z\right].$$ It must be emphasized that ${\binom{n}{p}}_{k}$ is not defined for $p>n$, and that the generating function (2.1) is only valid for $0 \le p \le n$.

An explicit expression is known for $G_n(y,z)$, but we shall not need it. With $x=z/(1-z)$, i.e. $z= x/(1+x)$, we have $$\begin{gathered} G_n(y,z)= 2^{-n} {\big( (1+x)(1+y)+\sqrt{(1+x)^2(1+y)^2-4y(1+x)} \big)}^n\\ + 2^{-n} {\big( (1+x)(1+y)-\sqrt{(1+x)^2(1+y)^2-4y(1+x)} \big)}^n -1-y^n.\end{gathered}$$

New coefficients

The following notion has been introduced in previous papers. For $\lambda$ a partition and any integer $k \ge 1$, let $\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{k}$ denote the number of ways to choose $k$ different cells in the Ferrers diagram of $\lambda$, taking at least one cell from each row. It is easily seen that $$\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{k}= \sum_{(k_i)}\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \binom{\lambda_i}{k_i}$$ the sum being taken over all decompositions $k=\sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} k_i$ with $k_i \neq 0$ for any $i$. The generating function for $\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{k}$ is the following $$\begin{split} \sum_{r \ge 1} \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{r}\,x^{r} &= \prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \left({(1 + x)}^{\lambda_i} - 1\right)\\ &= \prod_{i \ge 1} {\left({{(1 + x)}^i - 1}\right)}^{m_i(\lambda)}. \end{split}$$

Now in a strictly parallel way, for any integers $0 \le p \le |\lambda|$ and $k \ge 1$, we define $${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}= \sum_{(p_i)} \sum_{(k_i)} \prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} {\binom{\lambda_i}{p_i}}_{k_i}$$ the sum being taken over all decompositions $p=\sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} p_i$, $k=\sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} k_i$ with $0 \le p_i \le \lambda_i$ and $k_i \neq 0$ for any $i$. Observe that there is no such restriction for $p_i$.

This definition yields easily $${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}=0 \quad \textrm{except if} \quad l(\lambda) \le k \le |\lambda|.$$ Indeed it is obvious that ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}=0$ for $k<l(\lambda)$, and since ${\binom{n}{p}}_{k} = 0$ for $k>n$, we have also ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}=0$ for $k>|\lambda|$. For instance ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{1}=0$ except if $\lambda$ is a row partition $(n)$. In this case we have ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{(n)}{p}}_{k}={\binom{n}{p}}_{k}$.

We have obviously $${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{0}}_{k}= \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{k} \quad, \quad {\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{1}}_{k}= k \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{k},$$ and also $${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}={\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{|\lambda|-p}}_{k}.$$ Finally it is not difficult to check that $${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{|\lambda|}=\binom{|\lambda|}{p} \quad,\quad {\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{|\lambda|-1}=(|\lambda|-m_1(\lambda)) \left[\binom{|\lambda|-1}{p}+\binom{|\lambda|-2}{p-2}\right].$$ For instance the first relation is a direct consequence of the Chu-Vandermonde formula. Indeed the definition easily implies $${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{|\lambda|}= \sum_{(p_i)}\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} {\binom{\lambda_i}{p_i}}_{\lambda_i} = \sum_{(p_i)}\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \binom{\lambda_i}{p_i}.$$

As a straightforward consequence of their definition, the generating function for the numbers ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}$ is the following $$\sum_{p=0}^{|\lambda|} \sum_{k=l(\lambda)}^{|\lambda|} {\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k} y^p {\left(\frac{z}{1-z}\right)}^k =\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} G_{\lambda_i}(y,z) =\prod_{i \ge 1} {\Big(G_i(y,z) \Big)}^{m_i(\lambda)}.$$ One has easily $G_i(0,\frac{x}{1+x})=(1+x)^i-1$. Thus for $y=0$ we recover the generating function of ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{0}}_{k}= \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{k}$.

It must be emphasized that ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}$ is not defined for $p>|\lambda|$. An interesting problem is to get a combinatorial interpretation of ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\lambda}{p}}_{k}$.

Auxiliary polynomials

Let $X=(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots)$ be (infinitely many) independent indeterminates. In for any integers $n,k \ge 1$ we have defined $$P_{nk}(X)=\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{k}}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{i \ge 1}{X_{i}}^{m_{i}(\mu)}.$$ For $k=0$ we got $P_{n0}(X)=0$ ($n \neq 0$), and $P_{00}(X)=1$.

In a strictly parallel way, for any integers $n \ge 1$, $k \ge 1$ and $0 \le p \le n$ we set $$P_{npk}(X)=\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{i \ge 1}{X_{i}}^{m_{i}(\mu)}.$$ Since ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}=0$ for $k<l(\mu)$, this sum is restricted to partitions such that $l(\mu) \le k$. Hence $P_{npk}(X)$ is a polynomial in $X$. Similarly since ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}=0$ for $k>|\mu|$, one has $P_{npk}(X)=0$ for $k>n$.

For $k=0$ it is natural to extend the previous definition by the convention $P_{np0}(X)=0$ with the only exception $P_{000}(X)=1$. It must be emphasized that $P_{npk}(X)$ is not defined for $p > n$.

For $k=1$ we have $P_{np1}(X)=X_n$ and for $k=n$ $$P_{npn}(X)= \binom{n}{p} \sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{i \ge 1}{X_{i}}^{m_{i}(\mu)}=\binom{n}{p}P_{nn}(X).$$ Finally we have $P_{n0k}(X)= P_{nk}(X)$ and $P_{n1k}(X)= kP_{nk}(X)$. It is also obvious that $P_{npk}(X)=P_{n,n-p,k}(X)$.

Main identity

Let $X_{0}$ and $X=(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots)$ be (infinitely many) independent indeterminates. We give the explicit evaluation of $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_\mu}\prod_{k \ge 1} (S_k)^{m_k(\mu)},$$ when the formal series $S_k$ is chosen to be $$S_k=\sum_{r,s \ge 0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\,\frac{(k)_s}{s!}\, X_{r+s}.$$

For any integer $n \ge 1$ we have $$\begin{gathered} \sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(\sum_{r,s \ge 0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\,\frac{(k)_s}{s!}\, X_{r+s}\right)}^{m_{k}(\mu)} =\\ \sum_{p,q \ge 0} u^p v^q \left( \sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{X_{0}+n-1}{n-k} P_{p+q,p,k}(X) \right).\end{gathered}$$

Denote by $L(n)$ (resp. $R(n)$) the left (resp. right)-hand side of this identity. On the right-hand side, with $b=a/(1-a)$ and $w=u/v$, we get $$\begin{split} \sum_{n \ge 1} a^n R(n) &= \sum_{p,q \ge 0} u^p v^q \sum_{k = 0}^{p+q} \left( \sum_{n \ge k} a^n \binom{X_0+n-1}{n-k} \right) P_{p+q,p,k}(X) \\ & = (1-a)^{-X_0} \sum_{p,q \ge 0} u^p v^q \sum_{k = 0}^{p+q} b^k \left( \sum_{|\mu|=p+q} \frac{{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{i \ge 1}{X_i}^{m_i(\mu)} \right)\\ & = (1-a)^{-X_0} \sum_{\mu} v^{|\mu|} \sum_{p = 0}^{|\mu|} \sum_{k = 0}^{|\mu|} w^p b^k \frac{{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{i \ge 1}{X_i}^{m_i(\mu)}. \end{split}$$ Using the generating function (2.3) for ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}$, we obtain $$\begin{split} \sum_{n \ge 1} a^n R(n) &= (1-a)^{-X_0} \sum_{m_1,m_2,\ldots \ge 0} \prod_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{m_k!} {\left( v^k \frac{X_k}{k} \ G_k(w,a) \right)}^{m_k}\\ &=(1-a)^{-X_0} \prod_{k \ge 1} \textrm{exp} \left( v^k \frac{X_k}{k} \ G_k(w,a) \right)\\ &=(1-a)^{-X_0} \textrm{exp} \left( \sum_{k \ge 1} v^k \frac{X_k}{k} \ G_k(w,a) \right). \end{split}$$ On the left-hand side of the identity we have $$\begin{split} \sum_{n \ge 1} a^n L(n) &= \sum_{\mu} \frac{a^{|\mu|}}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(X_{0}+\sum_{t \ge 1} X_{t} \, \sum_{r=0}^t u^r v^{t-r} \frac{(k)_r}{r!} \, \frac{(k)_{t-r}}{(t-r)!} \right)}^{m_{k}(\mu)}\\ &= \sum_{m_1,m_2,\ldots \ge 0} \prod_{k \ge 1} \frac{1}{m_k!} {\left[\frac{a^k}{k} \left(X_{0}+\sum_{t \ge 1} v^t X_{t} \, \sum_{r=0}^t w^r \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\, \frac{(k)_{t-r}}{(t-r)!} \right)\right]}^{m_k}\\ &=(1-a)^{-X_0} \prod_{k \ge 1} \textrm{exp} \left(\frac{a^k}{k} \sum_{t \ge 1} v^t X_{t} \, \sum_{r=0}^t w^r \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\, \frac{(k)_{t-r}}{(t-r)!} \right)\\ &=(1-a)^{-X_0} \textrm{exp}\left[ \sum_{t \ge 1} v^t X_{t} \, \sum_{r=0}^t w^r \left( \sum_{k \ge 1} \frac{a^k}{k} \, \frac{(k)_r}{r!} \, \frac{(k)_{t-r}}{(t-r)!} \right) \right]. \end{split}$$ Thus it is enough to prove $$G_n(w,a) = n \sum_{r=0}^n w^r \left( \sum_{i \ge 1} \frac{a^i}{i}\, \frac{(i)_r}{r!} \, \frac{(i)_{n-r}}{(n-r)!} \right).$$ But obviously $$\sum_{i \ge 1} \frac{a^i}{i}\, \frac{(i)_r}{r!} \, \frac{(i)_{n-r}}{(n-r)!} = a \,{}_2F_1\!\left[\begin{matrix}r+1,n-r+1\\ 2\end{matrix};a\right].$$ We conclude by applying relation (2.2).

Theorem 3.1 immediatly yields $$\begin{gathered} \sum_{|\mu| = n} (-1)^{n-l(\mu)}\frac{1}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(\sum_{r,s \ge 0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\,\frac{(k)_s}{s!}\, X_{r+s}\right)}^{m_{k}(\mu)} =\\ \sum_{p,q \ge 0} u^p v^q \left( \sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} {(-1)}^k\binom{X_{0}-k}{n-k} P_{p+q,p,k}(-X) \right).\end{gathered}$$ It is an open question whether the right-hand side may be expressed in terms of the quantities $P_{p+q,p,k}(X)$. This is the case for $v=0$ (, Theorem 2, p. 301). Then one has $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} (-1)^{n-l(\mu)} \frac{1}{z_\mu} \prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(\sum_{r \ge 0}u^r\frac{(k)_r}{r!} X_r \right)}^{m_k(\mu)} = \sum_{p \ge 0} u^p\left( \sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p)} \binom{X_0-p}{n-k} P_{pk}(X) \right).$$ This is a consequence of the following non trivial property (, Corollaire 5), $$\sum_{k=l(\mu)}^{\mathrm{min}(n,|\mu|)} \binom{X_0-|\mu|}{n-k} \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{k}= \sum_{k=l(\mu)}^{\mathrm{min}(n,|\mu|)} (-1)^{k-l(\mu)} \binom{X_0-k}{n-k} \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{k}.$$ It would be interesting to obtain a generalization of this identity for ${\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}$.

First specialization

Various applications of Theorem 3.1 may be obtained by using different specia-lizations of the indeterminates $X_i$. In this section we shall consider the simplest case, obtained when all the $X_i, i\ge 0$ are equal.

Let $x$ be an indeterminate. In (Theorem 1, p. 461) we gave a bijective proof (due to Rodica Simion) of the identity $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} \genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{k}\frac{x^{l(\mu)}}{z_\mu}= \binom{n-1}{k-1}\binom{x + k - 1}{k}.$$ Since the Stirling numbers of the first kind $s(k,r)$ are defined by the generating function $$(x)_k =\sum_{r\ge1} |s(k,r)| \,x^r,$$ this identity is equivalent to $$\binom{n-1}{k-1} |s(k,r)|= k! \, \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mu|=n\\l(\mu) = r\end{subarray}} \frac{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{k}}{z_{\mu}}.$$

We generalize this result as follows (the previous case may be recovered by choosing $p=0$).

Let $x$ be an indeterminate. For any nonnegative integers $n,p,r$, we have $$\sum_{|\mu| = n} {\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}\frac{x^{l(\mu)}}{z_\mu}= \frac{k}{n}{\binom{n}{p}}_{k}\binom{x + k - 1}{k}.$$

With the specialization $X_i=x$ for any $i\ge 0$, the left-hand side of the identity of Theorem 3.1 reads $$\begin{split} \sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{1}{z_{\mu}}\prod_{k \ge 1} {\left(\sum_{r,s \ge 0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\,\frac{(k)_s}{s!}\, x \right)}^{m_{k}(\mu)} &= \sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{x^{l(\mu)}}{z_{\mu}} \prod_{k \ge 1}{\left((1-u)^{-k}\,(1-v)^{-k}\, \right)}^{m_{k}(\mu)}\\ &=\binom{x+n-1}{n} (1-u)^{-n}\,(1-v)^{-n}\\ &=\binom{x+n-1}{n} \left(\sum_{p,q \ge 0} u^p v^q \frac{(n)_p}{p!}\,\frac{(n)_q}{q!} \right). \end{split}$$ By identification of the coefficients in $u$ and $v$, we immediatly obtain for $p,q > 0$, $$\begin{split} \binom{x+n-1}{n} \frac{(n)_p}{p!}\,\frac{(n)_q}{q!} &= \sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{x+n-1}{n-k} P_{p+q,p,k}(x,\ldots,x) \\ &=\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{x+n-1}{n-k} \left(\sum_{|\mu| = p+q} {\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}\frac{x^{l(\mu)}}{z_\mu}\right). \end{split}$$ On the other hand, it is easily proved that we have $$\binom{x+n-1}{n} \frac{(n)_p}{p!}\,\frac{(n)_q}{q!} =\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{x+n-1}{n-k} \frac{k}{p+q}{\binom{p+q}{p}}_{k}\binom{x + k - 1}{k},$$ equivalently $$\frac{(n)_p}{p!}\,\frac{(n)_q}{q!} =\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{n}{k} \frac{k}{p+q} {\binom{p+q}{p}}_{k}.$$ Indeed for $p=0$ this is the classical Chu-Vandermonde formula. The property is then a direct consequence of the following recurrence relation (, Lemma 3.2) $$p{\binom{p+q}{p}}_k =(q+1){\binom{p+q}{p-1}}_k -\frac{p+q}{p+q-1}(q-p+1){\binom{p+q-1}{p-1}}_k.$$ But now if for a sequence of functions $f_k^{(pq)}(x),1 \le k\le p+q$, the relation $$\sum_{k=1}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{x+n-1}{n-k} f_k^{(pq)}(x)=0$$ is satisfied for any $n \ge 1$, by choosing successively $n=1,2,\ldots,p+q$ one has iteratively $f_k^{(pq)}=0$, and we can conclude.

Theorem 4.1 can be equivalently stated as $$\frac{k}{n}{\binom{n}{p}}_{k} |s(k,r)| = k! \, \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mu|=n\\l(\mu) = r\end{subarray}} \frac{{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}}{z_{\mu}}.$$ It would be interesting to obtain a bijective proof, in the same vein than Simion’s.

Main specialization

We now consider another specialization of Theorem 3.1 in the framework of (shifted) Jack polynomials.

Let $\alpha$ be some positive real number, and $\lambda$ an arbitrary partition. For any cell $(i,j)$ of $\lambda$ we define the “$\alpha$-content” $$c_{ij}^{\alpha}= j-1-(i-1)/\alpha.$$ We consider the following natural generalization of the “raising” and “lowering factorial” $$(x)_{\lambda}=\prod_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \left(x+c_{ij}^{\alpha}\right) \quad,\quad [x]_{\lambda}=\prod_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \left(x-c_{ij}^{\alpha}\right).$$ For any integer $k\ge 0$ we define $$d_{k}(\lambda) = \sum_{(i,j) \in \lambda} {(c_{ij}^{\alpha})}^k.$$ For any integers $n,p,k \ge 0$ we set $$F_{npk}(\lambda) = P_{npk}(d_{1}(\lambda),d_{2}(\lambda),d_{3}(\lambda),\ldots) =\sum_{|\mu| = n} \frac{{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{p}}_{k}}{z_{\mu}}\, d_\mu(\lambda)$$ and $F_{nk}(\lambda)=F_{n0k}(\lambda)$, with the obvious notation $$d_\mu(\lambda)= \prod_{i \ge 1} d_i(\lambda)^{m_i(\mu)}.$$ In other words we choose the following specialization $$X_0=d_{0}(\lambda)=|\lambda| \quad,\quad X_{k}=d_{k}(\lambda) \quad (k \ge 1),$$ though the quantities $d_{k}(\lambda)$ are no longer independent indeterminates.

In we have shown the following development $$\frac{(x+y)_{\lambda}}{(y)_{\lambda}} = \sum_{i,j\ge 0} (-1)^{j} \frac{x^i}{y^{i+j}} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(i,j)}\binom{|\lambda|-j}{i-k}\,F_{jk}(\lambda) \right),$$ where the sum takes over any $j\ge 0$ and not only over $|\lambda|-j\ge 0$.

An analogous result can be deduced from Theorem 3.1.

Let $x,y$ be two indeterminates. Then we have $$\begin{gathered} \frac{(x+y+1)_{\lambda}}{(x+y)_{\lambda}}\, \frac{(x)_{\lambda}}{(x+1)_{\lambda}} = \sum_{n\ge 0} {\Big(-\frac{y}{x^2}\Big)}^n {\Big(1+\frac{y+1}{x}\Big)}^{-n}\\ \sum_{p,q \ge 0} {\Big(\frac{-1}{x}\Big)}^{p+q} {\Big(1+\frac{y+1}{x}\Big)}^{-q}\left( \sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{|\lambda|+n-1}{n-k} F_{p+q,p,k}(\lambda) \right).\end{gathered}$$

With $c_{ij}=c_{ij}^{\alpha}$ for short, the left-hand side can be written $$\begin{split} \textrm{LHS}&=\prod_{(i,j)\in \lambda} \frac{(x+y+1+c_{ij})}{(x+y+c_{ij})} \, \frac{(x+c_{ij})}{(x+1+c_{ij})}\\ &= \prod_{(i,j)\in \lambda} {\Big(1+\frac{y}{(x+y+1+c_{ij}) (x+c_{ij})}\Big)}^{-1}. \end{split}$$ Setting $u=-1/x$, $v=-1/(x+y+1)$, and using the classical series expansion $$\textrm{log}(1-a)=-\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{a^k}{k},$$ we get $$\begin{split} \textrm{LHS}&=\prod_{(i,j)\in \lambda} \textrm{exp} \Big[ \sum_{k\ge1}\frac{(-y)^k}{k}{\Big((x+y+1+c_{ij})(x+c_{ij})\Big)}^{-k}\Big]\\ &= \textrm{exp} \Big[\sum_{(i,j)\in \lambda} \Big(\sum_{k\ge1} \frac{(-yuv)^k}{k} {(1-c_{ij} u)}^{-k} {(1-c_{ij} v)}^{-k}\Big)\Big]. \end{split}$$ Then using the series expansion $${(1-a)}^{-k}=\sum_{r\ge0} a^r \frac{(k)_r}{r!},$$ we obtain $$\begin{split} \textrm{LHS}&= \textrm{exp} \Big[ \sum_{k\ge1} \frac{(-yuv)^k}{k} \Big( \sum_{r,s\ge0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!} \frac{(k)_s}{s!} d_{r+s}(\lambda)\Big)\Big]\\ &= \prod_{k\ge1} \Big( \sum_{m_k\ge0} \frac{1}{m_k!} {\Big[ \frac{(-yuv)^k}{k} \Big( \sum_{r,s\ge0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!} \, \frac{(k)_s}{s!} \, d_{r+s}(\lambda) \Big) \Big]}^{m_k} \Big)\\ &=\sum_\mu \frac{(-yuv)^{|\mu|}}{z_{\mu}} \prod_{k\ge1} {\Big(\sum_{r,s\ge0} u^r v^s \frac{(k)_r}{r!}\, \frac{(k)_s}{s!}\, d_{r+s}(\lambda)\Big)}^{m_k(\mu)}. \end{split}$$ We conclude by applying Theorem 3.1 with the specialization $X_{k}=d_{k}(\lambda)$, which gives $$\textrm{LHS}=\sum_{n\ge 0} (-yuv)^n \sum_{p,q \ge 0} u^p v^q \left( \sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,p+q)} \binom{|\lambda|+n-1}{n-k} F_{p+q,p,k}(\lambda) \right).$$

Let $x,y$ be two indeterminates. Then we have $$\frac{(x+y+1)_{\lambda}}{(x+y)_{\lambda}}\, \frac{(x)_{\lambda}}{(x+1)_{\lambda}} = \sum_{r\ge 0} c_r{\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right)}^r$$ with $$c_{r}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n,p,q \ge 0 \\ 2n+p+q \le r\end{subarray}} (-y)^n (y+1)^p\binom{n+p+q-1}{p} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,r-2n-p)} \binom{|\lambda|+n-1}{n-k} F_{r-2n-p,q,k}(\lambda) \right).$$

Observe the situation for low indices. One has $c_0 =1$ since $F_{000}(\lambda)=1$, and $c_1=0$ since $F_{1q0}(\lambda)=0$.

This result is useful in the study of Jack polynomials, allowing to prove some conjectures stated in. The proofs will be given in Sections 8 and 9.

Symmetric functions

Let $A=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots\}$ a (possibly infinite) set of independent indeterminates ($A$ is called an alphabet). The generating functions $$\begin{split} E_t(A) &= \prod_{a\in A} (1 +ta) =\sum_{k\geq0} t^k\, e_k(A)\\ H_t(A) &= \prod_{a\in A} \frac{1}{1-ta} = \sum_{k\geq0} t^k\, h_k(A)\\ P_t(A) &= \sum_{a\in A} \frac{a}{1-ta} =\sum_{k\geq1} t^{k-1}p_k(A) \end{split}$$ define symmetric functions known as respectively elementary, complete and power sums. For any partition $\mu$, we define functions $e_\mu$, $h_\mu$ or $p_\mu$ by $$f_{\mu}= \prod_{i=1}^{l(\mu)}f_{\mu_{i}}=\prod_{k\geq1}f_k^{m_{k}(\mu)},$$ where $f_{i}$ stands for $e_i$, $h_i$ or $p_i$. The monomial symmetric function $m_\mu(A)$ is defined as the sum of all distincts monomials $\prod_{i}a_i^{m_i}$ such that $(m_i)$ is a permutation of $\mu$.

When $A$ is infinite, each of the three sets of functions $e_i(A)$, $h_i(A)$ or $p_i(A)$ forms an algebraic basis of $\mathbf{S}[A]$, the symmetric functions algebra of $A$. Each of the sets of functions $e_\mu(A)$, $h_\mu(A)$, $p_\mu(A)$ is a linear basis of this algebra. It is thus possible to define the symmetric algebra $\mathbf{S}$ abstractly, as the $\mathbf{R}$-algebra generated by the functions $e_i$, $h_i$ or $p_i$.

This is no longer true when $A$ is finite, a situation which is often encountered. In that case the functions $e_\mu(A)$ (resp. $h_\mu(A)$, $p_\mu(A)$) are no longer linearly independent. We have encountered such a situation with the previous specialization $X_k=d_k(\lambda)$. Let $$A_\lambda=\left\{c_{ij}^{\alpha}=j-1-(i-1)/\alpha,\quad (i,j) \in \lambda\right\}$$ denote the finite alphabet of $\alpha$-contents of $\lambda$. By definition we have $$d_k(\lambda)=p_k(A_\lambda) \quad (k \ge 1),\quad d_\mu(\lambda)=p_\mu(A_\lambda).$$

Thus the left-hand sides of the relation of Theorem 5.1, as well as of relation (5.1), are symmetric functions of the alphabet $A_\lambda$. The expressions given are in terms of the power-sums $p_\mu(A_\lambda)$, but it might be also interesting to convert them in terms of any other symmetric functions of $A_\lambda$.

With this conversion in mind, we are led to the two following open problems. Let $A=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots\}$ be any (finite or infinite) alphabet. Choose the specialization $X_k = p_k(A), \, (k\ge 1)$. By definition for any $n,k \ge 0$ we have $$P_{nk}(-X) = \sum_{|\mu| = n} (-1)^{l(\mu)} \frac{\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\mu}{k}}{z_\mu}\, p_\mu(A).$$ In (Lemma 2, p. 306) we have shown $$P_{nk}(-X) = (-1)^{k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mu| = n\\ l(\mu) = k\end{subarray}} m_{\mu} (A).$$ Let $\omega$ be the involution defined by $\omega(p_r)= (-1)^{r-1} p_r$. One has $\omega(P_{nk}(X)) =(-1)^n P_{nk}(-X)$, hence $$P_{nk}(X) = (-1)^{n-k}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mu| = n\\ l(\mu) = k\end{subarray}} f_{\mu} (A),$$ with $f_{\mu}$ the fourth classical basis of “forgotten”symmetric functions (, p. 22).

Evaluate $P_{npk}(-X)$ in terms of monomial symmetric functions of $A$.

Using ACE there is some experimental evidence that $$P_{npk}(-X) = (-1)^{k} \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}|\mu| = n\\ l(\mu) = k\end{subarray}} \chi_{\mu}\,m_{\mu} (A),$$ with $\chi_{\mu}$ some polynomial in the multiplicities of $\mu$. It seems that for $p \le 3$ one has $$\chi_{\mu}= \binom{k+p-1}{p}-\binom{k+p-3}{p-2} m_1(\mu)- \binom{k+p-4}{p-3} m_2(\mu).$$

Now if we define the alphabet $$B_0=\{a_1/(1-a_1),a_2/(1-a_2),a_3/(1-a_3),\ldots\},$$ it was proved in (Theorem 2) that for any $k\ge 1$, one has $$\begin{split} p_k(B_0) = \sum_{n\ge k} &\binom{n-1}{k-1} p_{n}(A)\\ h_k(B_0) = \sum_{n\ge k}P_{nk}(X) \quad&,\quad e_k(B_0) = (-1)^k \sum_{n\ge k}P_{nk}(-X). \end{split}$$

For any integer $p\ge 0$, find an alphabet $B_p$ such that for any $k\ge 1$, $$p_k(B_p) = \sum_{n\ge \mathrm{max}(k,p)} \frac{k}{n} \, {\binom{n}{p}}_{k} p_{n}(A).$$ Give the expansion of $h_k(B_p)$ (resp. $e_k(B_p)$) in terms of the quantities $P_{npk}(X)$ (resp. $P_{npk}(-X)$).

For any two alphabets $A$ and $B$, their difference $A-B$ (which is not their difference as sets) is defined by $$E_t(A-B) = E_t(A)\,{E_t(B)}^{-1} \quad,\quad H_t(A-B) = H_t(A)\,{H_t(B)}^{-1}.$$ In Sections 8 and 9 we shall need the following result about Lagrange interpolation.

Let $A$ and $B$ be two finite alphabets with respective cardinals $n$ and $m$. For any integer $r\ge0$ we have $$\sum_{a \in A} a^r \, \frac{\displaystyle\prod_{b \in B}(a-b)} {\displaystyle\prod_{c \in A, \, c \neq a} (a-c)} = h_{m-n+r+1}(A-B).$$

Alain Lascoux mentions that when $B$ is empty, this result was already known to Euler.

Shifted symmetric functions

Though the theory of symmetric functions goes back to the early 19th century, the notion of “shifted symmetric” functions is very recent. We refer to, and to references given there. We shall follow the presentation given by.

Let $\alpha$ be some fixed positive real number and $\mathbf{F}$ be the field of rational functions in $\alpha$. A polynomial in $n$ variables $(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ with coefficients in $\mathbf{F}$ is said to be shifted symmetric if it is symmetric in the “shifted variables” $x_i-i/\alpha$. Let ${\mathbf{S}}_n^{*}$ denote this subalgebra of $\mathbf{F}[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n]$.

Now let $X=\{x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots\}$ be an infinite alphabet. Consider the morphism from ${\mathbf{S}}_{n+1}^{*}$ to ${\mathbf{S}}_n^{*}$ given by $x_{n+1}=0$. In analogy with symmetric functions, the shifted symmetric algebra $\mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$ is defined as the projective limit of the algebras ${\mathbf{S}}_n^{*}$ with respect to this morphism. In other words a “shifted symmetric function” $f\in \mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$ is a family $\{f_n, n\ge 1\}$ with the two following properties

 1. $f_n \in {\mathbf{S}}_n^{*}$ (shifted symmetry),

 2. $f_{n+1}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n,0)=f_{n}(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ (stability).

For instance if for any integer $k\ge 1$ we define the “shifted power sums” by $$p_k^{*}(x)=\sum_{i\ge 1}\Big([x_i-(i-1)/\alpha]_k-[-(i-1)/\alpha]_k\Big),$$ these polynomials algebraically generate ${\mathbf{S}}^{*}[X]$.

Any element $f\in \mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$ may be evaluated at any sequence $x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots)$ with finitely many non zero terms, hence at any partition $\lambda$. Moreover by analyticity, $f$ is entirely determined by its restriction $f(\lambda)$ to partitions. From now on we shall perform this identification, and consider $\mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$ as a function algebra $\mathbf{S}^{*}[\mathcal{P}]$ on the set $\mathcal{P}$ of partitions. In this approach, a partition is no longer a parameter but an argument. The following lemma is crucial (, p. 151). The argument is taken from (Lemma 7.1).

For any integer $k\ge 1$, the function $\lambda\rightarrow d_k(\lambda)$ defines a shifted symmetric function.

Let $t(k,m)$ denote the inverse matrix of $s(k,m)$, the matrix of Stirling numbers of the first kind, that is $x^k=\sum_{m=1}^kt(k,m)[x]_{m}$. We have $$d_k= \sum_{m=1}^k t(k,m) \frac{p_{m+1}^{*}}{m+1}.$$ Indeed we can write $$\begin{split} d_k(\lambda)&= \sum_{m=1}^k \sum_{(i,j)\in \lambda} t(k,m)\, [j-1-(i-1)/\alpha]_{m}\\ &= \sum_{m=1}^k \frac{t(k,m)}{m+1} \sum_{i= 1}^{l(\lambda)} \Big([\lambda_i-(i-1)/\alpha]_{m+1}-[-(i-1)/\alpha]_{m+1}\Big), \end{split}$$ the last equation being a direct consequence of the identity $m[x]_{m-1}=[x+1]_{m}-[x]_{m}$.

For instance we have $$d_1=\frac{p_2^{*}}{2} \quad,\quad d_2= \frac{p_3^{*}}{3}+\frac{p_2^{*}}{2} \quad,\quad d_3= \frac{p_4^{*}}{4}+p_3^{*}+\frac{p_2^{*}}{2}.$$

For each element $f\in \mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$ we define its so called leading symmetric term $[f]\in \mathbf{S}[X]$ as the highest degree homogeneous part of $f$. For instance we have $[p_k^{\star}]=p_k$. The map $f\rightarrow [f]$ provides an isomorphism of the graded algebra associated to the filtered algebra $\mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$ onto the symmetric function algebra $\mathbf{S}[X]$. Assuming that the leading terms $[f_1],[f_2],\ldots,[f_n]$ of a sequence $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_n$ generate $\mathbf{S}[X]$, then this sequence itself generates $\mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$.

Now for $k\ge1$ as a consequence of Lemma 7.1, $$[d_k]=\frac{[p_{k+1}^{*}]}{k+1} =\frac{p_{k+1}}{k+1}.$$ Thus the shifted symmetric functions $p_1^{*}=p_1$ and $d_k, k\ge 1$ algebraically generate $\mathbf{S}^{*}[X]$. In other words any $f\in \mathbf{S}^{*}[\mathcal{P}]$ may be expanded in terms of the functions $|\lambda|^r d_\mu(\lambda)$ with $r\ge0$ and $\mu$ any partition.

But as seen before $d_\mu(\lambda)=p_\mu(A_\lambda)$ and there is no reason that we shall restrict to the basis of power sums in the alphabet $A_\lambda$. Any other basis of the symmetric algebra may be convenient. Therefore any $f\in \mathbf{S}^{*}[\mathcal{P}]$ may be expanded in terms of the functions $|\lambda|^r b_\mu(A_\lambda)$, with $r\ge0$ and $b_\mu$ any linear basis of the symmetric algebra $\mathbf{S}$, viewed abstractly.

Finally we have proved

Let $G=\mathbf{F}[w]$ be the field of polynomials in some indeterminate $w$ with coefficients in $\mathbf{F}$. The evaluation map $p\otimes f \rightarrow p(|\lambda|)f(A_\lambda)$ is an isomorphism of $G\otimes\mathbf{S}$ onto $\mathbf{S}^{*}[\mathcal{P}]$.

Let us give a simple but enlightening example. Recall that the generalized raising and lowering factorial are given by $$(x)_{\lambda}=\prod_{a \in A_{\lambda}} (x+a) \quad,\quad [x]_{\lambda}=\prod_{a \in A_{\lambda}} (x-a).$$ Then let us define (, p. 64) $$(x)_{\lambda}= \sum_{k\geq 0} c_k(\lambda) \, x^{|\lambda|-k} \quad, \quad \frac{1}{[x]_{\lambda}}= \sum_{k\geq 0} C_k(\lambda) \, \frac{1}{x^{|\lambda|+k}}.$$ The quantities $c_k(\lambda)$ and $C_k(\lambda)$ are generalizations of Stirling numbers of the first and second kind, since when $\lambda$ is a row-partition $(n)$, they are respectively $|s(n,k)|$ and $S(n+k-1,n-1)$.

We know immediatly that $c_k(\lambda)$ and $C_k(\lambda)$ are shifted symmetric functions, i.e. belong to $\mathbf{S}^{*}[\mathcal{P}]$, and that they satisfy $$c_k(\lambda)=\sum_{|\mu|=k} (-1)^{k-l(\mu)} \frac{1}{z_\mu} \, d_\mu(\lambda) \quad, \quad C_k(\lambda)=\sum_{|\mu|=k} \frac{1}{z_\mu} \, d_\mu(\lambda).$$ Indeed their definition are merely the generating functions for elementary and complete symmetric functions of the alphabet $A_{\lambda}$ since $$\begin{split} (x)_{\lambda}=\prod_{a \in A_{\lambda}} (x+a) &= x^{|\lambda|} E_{1/x}(A_\lambda) = \sum_{k\geq0} x^{|\lambda|-k}\, e_k(A_\lambda)\\ \frac{1}{[x]_{\lambda}}=\prod_{a \in A_{\lambda}} \frac{1}{x-a} &=\frac{1}{x^{|\lambda|}} H_{1/x}(A_\lambda) = \sum_{k\geq0} \frac{1}{x^{|\lambda|+k}}\, h_k(A_\lambda). \end{split}$$ Thus it is enough to apply the classical Cauchy formulas (, p. 25) to get $$\begin{split} c_k(\lambda)=e_k(A_\lambda)&=\sum_{|\mu|=k} (-1)^{k-l(\mu)} \frac{1}{z_\mu} \, p_\mu(A_\lambda)\\ C_k(\lambda)=h_k(A_\lambda)&=\sum_{|\mu|=k} \frac{1}{z_\mu} \, p_\mu(A_\lambda). \end{split}$$

Application to Jack polynomials

The reference for Jack polynomials is Chapter 6, Section 10 of the book of Macdonald. Let $\alpha$ be some fixed positive real number. Jack polynomials $J_\lambda^{\alpha}$ form a basis of $\mathbf{F}\otimes\mathbf{S}$, the algebra of symmetric functions with coefficients in $\mathbf{F}$.

Jack polynomials satisfy the following generalization of Pieri formula. For any partition $\lambda$ and any integer $i$ such that $1 \le i \le l(\lambda)+1$, denote $\lambda^{(i)}$ the partition $\mu$, if it exists, such that $\mu_j=\lambda_j$ for $j\neq i$ and $\mu_i=\lambda_i +1$. Then we have $$e_1 \,J_\lambda^{\alpha} =\sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)+1} c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda) \, J_{\lambda^{(i)}}^{\alpha}.$$ The Pieri coefficients $c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda)$ have the following analytic expression $$c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda) = \frac {1}{\alpha \lambda_i+l(\lambda)-i+2} \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1 \\ j \neq i\end{subarray}}^{l(\lambda)+1} \frac{\alpha(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)+j-i+1} {\alpha(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)+j-i}.$$

For any integer $r\ge 0$ we define $$s_r(\lambda) =\sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)+1} {\left(\lambda_i-\frac{i-1}{\alpha}\right)}^r c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda).$$ In we gave the values of $s_r(\lambda)$ up to $r=9$. For instance one has $$s_0(\lambda) = 1 \quad,\quad s_1(\lambda) = 0 \quad,\quad s_2(\lambda)=|\lambda|/\alpha \quad,\quad s_3(\lambda)=2d_1(\lambda)/\alpha + |\lambda|(\alpha-1)/\alpha^2.$$

Since $c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda)$ is a rational function of the variables $\{\lambda_i-i/\alpha\}$, it is not obvious that $s_r(\lambda)$ is a shifted symmetric function, i.e. a polynomial in $\{\lambda_i-i/\alpha\}$. A proof has been given by Macdonald (, Theorem 6.1, p. 69). A more direct proof is given below, together with a new explicit formula.

In (Conjecture 6.2, p. 70) we had stated the following conjecture.

For any partition $\lambda$ and any integer $r\ge 0$ one has $$s_r(\lambda) =\sum_{i= 0}^{[r/2]} \, \sum_{j=0}^{r-2i} \, \sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(i,j)} \frac{1}{\alpha^i} \left(1-\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^{r-2i-j} \binom{|\lambda|+i-1}{i-k} \sum_{|\rho|=j} u_{ijk}^{\rho} (r) \frac{d_\rho(\lambda)}{z_{\rho}},$$ where the coefficients $u_{ijk}^{\rho} (r)$ are positive integers.

The previous conjecture is true, with $$u_{ijk}^{\rho} (r) = \sum_{s=0}^j {\genfrac{\langle}{\rangle}{0pt}{}{\rho}{s}}_{k} \binom{r+s-i-j-1}{r-2i-j}.$$ In other words we have $$\begin{gathered} s_r(\lambda)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n,p,q \ge 0 \\ 2n+p+q \le r\end{subarray}} \frac{1}{\alpha^n} \left(1-\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^p \binom{n+p+q-1}{p}\\ \left(\sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,r-2n-p)} \binom{|\lambda|+n-1}{n-k} F_{r-2n-p,q,k}(\lambda) \right).\end{gathered}$$

We shall prove that the quantities $s_r(\lambda)$ have the following generating function $$\sum_{r\ge 0} s_r(\lambda){\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right)}^r =\frac{(x-1/\alpha+1)_{\lambda}}{(x-1/\alpha)_{\lambda}} \frac{(x)_{\lambda}}{(x+1)_{\lambda}}.$$ Then the statement will immediatly follow from Corollary 5.2 with $y=-1/\alpha$. To prove this generating function we apply Lagrange Lemma for the two following alphabets $$\begin{split} A=\{a_i =\alpha\lambda_i -i+1 &,\quad i=1,\ldots,l(\lambda)+1 \},\\ B=\{b_i =\alpha\lambda_i -i &,\quad i=1,\ldots,l(\lambda)\}. \end{split}$$ Then it is obvious that $$c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda)= \frac {\displaystyle \prod_{b \in B}(a_i-b)} {\displaystyle \prod_{c \in A,\, c \neq a_i}(a_i-c)},$$ and the Lagrange Lemma yields $$\alpha^r s_r(\lambda)= h_r(A-B).$$ The generating function of $\alpha^r s_r(\lambda)$ is thus $$\begin{split} H_z(A-B)&= \frac {\prod_{b\in B} (1-zb)}{\prod_{a\in A} (1-za)}\\ &=\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{1-z(\alpha\lambda_i -i)}{1-z(\alpha\lambda_i-i+1)} \, \frac{1}{1+zl(\lambda)}. \end{split}$$ With $\alpha z=-1/x$ we obtain $$\sum_{r\ge 0} s_r(\lambda){\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right)}^r = \prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{x+\lambda_i -i/\alpha}{x+\lambda_i -(i-1)/\alpha} \, \frac{x}{x-l(\lambda)/\alpha}.$$ Since $$\frac {(u+1)_\lambda}{(u)_\lambda}=\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \prod_{j=1}^{\lambda_i} \frac{u+j-(i-1)/\alpha}{u+j-1-(i-1)/\alpha} =\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{u+\lambda_i-(i-1)/\alpha}{u-(i-1)/\alpha}$$ we conclude easily.

As already emphasized, Theorem 8.1 gives the expansion of the shifted symmetric function $s_r(\lambda)$ over the basis $|\lambda|^r p_\mu(A_\lambda)$. An open problem is to find explicit expansions over different basis of the symmetric algebra $\mathbf{S}[A_{\lambda}]$, for instance $|\lambda|^r m_\mu(A_\lambda)$.

Application to shifted Jack polynomials

For any partition $\mu$ there exists a shifted symmetric function $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}$ such that

 1. degree $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}} = |\mu|$,

 2. $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\lambda)=0$ except if $\mu_i \le \lambda_i$ for any $i$, and $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\mu) \neq 0$.

This function is called the shifted Jack polynomial associated with $\mu$. It is unique up to the value of $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\mu)$. When conveniently normalized, $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\lambda)$ is merely the generalized binomial coefficient $$\frac{\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\lambda)}{\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\mu)} = {\binom{\lambda}{\mu}}_{\alpha}$$ appearing in the generalized binomial formula for Jack polynomials.

We mention the two following remarkable facts :

 1. In the definition of $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}$, the overdetermined system of linear conditions (ii) may be replaced by the weaker conditions

 2. $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\lambda)=0$ except if $|\mu| \le |\lambda|$, and $\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}(\mu) \neq 0$.

 3. For some constant $h_\mu$ one has $[\widetilde{J_\mu^{\alpha}}]= h_\mu J_\mu^{\alpha}$.

For any partition $\lambda$ and any integer $i$ such that $1 \le i \le l(\lambda)$, we denote $\lambda_{(i)}$ the partition $\mu$, if it exists, such that $\mu_j=\lambda_j$ for $j\neq i$ and $\mu_i=\lambda_i -1$. In, p. 320 (see also, Theorem 5), we have proved that $${\binom{\lambda}{\lambda_{(i)}}}_{\alpha} = \left(\lambda_i +\frac {l(\lambda)-i}{\alpha}\right) \prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1 \\ j \neq i \end{subarray}}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{\alpha(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)+j-i-1} {\alpha(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)+j-i}.$$ For any integer $r\ge 0$ we introduce the shifted symmetric function $$\sigma_r(\lambda) =\sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} {\left(\lambda_i-\frac{i-1}{\alpha}\right)}^r {\binom{\lambda}{\lambda_{(i)}}}_{\alpha}.$$ As shown in, Theorem 8 (see also, Theorem 3) we have $\sigma_0(\lambda)= |\lambda|$. But even the computation of the first values $$\sigma_1(\lambda) = 2d_1(\lambda) + |\lambda|\quad,\quad \sigma_2(\lambda) = 3d_2(\lambda) +\left(3+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)d_1(\lambda) + |\lambda|-\frac{1}{\alpha} \binom{|\lambda|}{2}$$ seems rather difficult, except by the method given below.

We have $$\sigma_r(\lambda)=c_{r+1}-\alpha \, c_{r+2},$$ with $$\begin{gathered} c_{r}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n,p,q \ge 0 \\ 2n+p+q \le r\end{subarray}} \left(-\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^n \left(1+\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)^p \binom{n+p+q-1}{p}\\ \left(\sum_{k=0}^{\mathrm{min}(n,r-2n-p)} \binom{|\lambda|+n-1}{n-k} F_{r-2n-p,q,k}(\lambda) \right).\end{gathered}$$

We shall prove that the quantities $\sigma_r(\lambda)$ have the following generating function $$\sum_{r\ge 0} \sigma_r(\lambda){\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right)}^r = -x(\alpha x+1)\, \left(\frac{(x+1/\alpha+1)_{\lambda}}{(x+1/\alpha)_{\lambda}} \frac{(x)_{\lambda}}{(x+1)_{\lambda}} -1\right)$$ Then the statement will immediatly follow from Corollary 5.2 with $y=1/\alpha$. To prove this generating function we apply Lagrange Lemma for the two following alphabets $$\begin{split} A=\{a_i =\alpha\lambda_i -i+1 &,\quad i=1,\ldots,l(\lambda) \},\\ B=\{b_i =\alpha\lambda_i -i+2 &,\quad i=1,\ldots,l(\lambda)+1\}. \end{split}$$ Then it is obvious that $${\binom{\lambda}{\lambda_{(i)}}}_{\alpha}= -\frac{1}{\alpha}\, \frac {\displaystyle \prod_{b \in B}(a_i-b)} {\displaystyle \prod_{c \in A,\, c \neq a_i}(a_i-c)},$$ and the Lagrange Lemma yields $$-\alpha^{r+1} \sigma_r(\lambda)= h_{r+2}(A-B).$$ The generating function of $-\alpha^{r+1} \sigma_r(\lambda)$ is thus $$-\sum_{r\ge 0} \alpha^{r+1} z^r \sigma_r(\lambda) = \frac{1}{z^2} \sum_{r\ge2}z^r h_{r}(A-B) = \frac{1}{z^2}\big(H_z(A-B)-zh_{1}(A-B)-1\big).$$ But we have $$\begin{split} H_z(A-B)&= \frac {\prod_{b\in B} (1-zb)}{\prod_{a\in A} (1-za)}\\ &=\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{1-z(\alpha\lambda_i -i+2)}{1-z(\alpha\lambda_i-i+1)} \, (1+z(l(\lambda)-1). \end{split}$$ And it is easily checked that $$h_{1}(A-B)= \sum_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} (a_i -b_i)+l(\lambda)-1=-1.$$ With $\alpha z=-1/x$ we obtain $$\sum_{r\ge 0} \sigma_r(\lambda){\left(\frac{-1}{x}\right)}^r = -\alpha x^2 \left( \prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{x+\lambda_i -(i-2)/\alpha}{x+\lambda_i -(i-1)/\alpha} \, \frac{x-(l(\lambda)-1)/\alpha}{x} -\frac{1}{\alpha x} -1 \right).$$ The right-hand side can be written as $$-\alpha x \, (x-(l(\lambda)-1)/\alpha) \, \frac{(x+1/\alpha+1)_{\lambda}}{(x+1/\alpha)_{\lambda}} \frac{(x)_{\lambda}}{(x+1)_{\lambda}}\,\prod_{i=1}^{l(\lambda)} \frac{x -(i-2)/\alpha}{x -(i-1)/\alpha} +x +\alpha x^2.$$ Hence the result.

Probability distributions

Let us briefly outline the connections of these results with probability distributions on the set of Young diagrams.

We denote by $\mathcal{P}_n$ the set of Young (i.e. Ferrers) diagrams with $n$ cells, and by $\mathcal{P}=\cup\, \mathcal{P}_n$ the lattice of all Young diagrams ordered by inclusion. We write $\lambda\nearrow \Lambda$ if the diagram $\Lambda$ is obtained from $\lambda$ by adding a cell, i.e. $\Lambda=\lambda^{(i)}$ for some row $i$. We consider such a pair $(\lambda,\Lambda)$ as an “oriented edge” of the “infinite graph” $\mathcal{P}$.

We use the Pieri formula $$e_1 \,J_\lambda^{\alpha} =\sum_{\Lambda :\lambda\nearrow \Lambda} \kappa(\lambda,\Lambda) \, J_{\Lambda}^{\alpha}.$$ to define a “multiplicity function” $\kappa$ on the set of edges of $\mathcal{P}$. A function $\Phi$ defined on $\mathcal{P}$ is said to be harmonic if for all vertices $\lambda\in\mathcal{P}$ one has $$\Phi(\lambda)=\sum_{\Lambda :\lambda\nearrow \Lambda} \kappa(\lambda,\Lambda) \, \Phi(\Lambda).$$ Let $\varphi$ be the particular case corresponding to the initial condition $\varphi(\emptyset) =1$. Then (, Lemma 7.2) one has $\varphi(\lambda) =1$ for any $\lambda\in\mathcal{P}$.

Similarly we define a “dimension function” $\mathrm{dim}\ \Lambda$ by the following recurrence $$\mathrm{dim}\ \Lambda=\sum_{\lambda:\lambda\nearrow \Lambda} \kappa(\lambda,\Lambda) \, \mathrm{dim}\ \lambda$$ with the initial condition $\mathrm{dim}\ \emptyset =1$. Then (, Corollary 6.10) one has $$\mathrm{dim}\ \lambda=|\lambda|! \, \frac{\alpha^{|\lambda|}}{j_\lambda^{\alpha}}$$ with $j_\lambda^{\alpha}=\langle J_\lambda^{\alpha},J_\lambda^{\alpha} \rangle$ the norm of $J_\lambda^{\alpha}$ (, p. 97).

It is shown in that for any oriented edge $\lambda\nearrow \Lambda$ the quantities $$p_{\lambda}(\Lambda)=\kappa(\lambda,\Lambda)\, \frac{\varphi(\Lambda)}{\varphi(\lambda)} \quad,\quad q_{\Lambda}(\lambda)=\kappa(\lambda,\Lambda)\, \frac{\mathrm{dim}\ \lambda}{\mathrm{dim}\ \Lambda}$$ define two discrete “transition” $p_{\lambda}$ and “co-transition” $q_{\Lambda}$ probability distributions, associated with the Young diagrams $\lambda$ and $\Lambda$ respectively.

But as a consequence of, Theorem 2 for any oriented edge $\lambda\nearrow \Lambda$ one has $$\kappa(\lambda,\Lambda)=\alpha \ \frac{j_\lambda^{\alpha}}{j_\Lambda^{\alpha}} \ {\binom{\Lambda}{\lambda}}_{\alpha},$$ so that with our previous notations, we can write $$p_{\lambda}(\lambda^{(i)})=c_i^{\alpha}(\lambda)\quad,\quad q_{\Lambda}(\Lambda_{(i)})=\frac{1}{|\Lambda|} {\binom{\Lambda}{\Lambda_{(i)}}}_{\alpha}.$$ Now let us consider the $\alpha$-content random variable $c$ defined on any cell $(i,j)$ by $c(i,j)=j-1-(i-1)/\alpha$. If $\lambda\nearrow \Lambda$ is an oriented edge (i.e. $\Lambda=\lambda^{(i)}$ for some row $i$) we have $$c(\Lambda \setminus\lambda)=\lambda_i-(i-1)/\alpha= \Lambda_i-1-(i-1)/\alpha.$$ Hence the moments of the random variable $c$ with respect to the transition and co-transition distributions are respectively $$\begin{split} M_{r}(c)&= \sum_{\Lambda :\lambda\nearrow \Lambda} {c(\Lambda \setminus\lambda)}^r \,p_{\lambda}(\Lambda)=s_r(\lambda),\\ \tilde{M}_{r}(c)&= \sum_{\lambda:\lambda\nearrow \Lambda} {c(\Lambda \setminus\lambda)}^r \,q_{\Lambda}(\lambda)= \frac{1}{|\Lambda|} \sum_{k=0}^r (-1)^{r-k} \binom{r}{k} \sigma_k(\Lambda). \end{split}$$ Our results in Sections 8 and 9 thus amount to give an explicit evaluation of these moments.

If $\alpha =1$ the multiplicities are given by $\kappa(\lambda,\Lambda)= H_{\lambda}/H_{\Lambda}$, with $H_{\lambda}$ the classical hook polynomial $\prod_{i,j \in \lambda}(\lambda_i+\lambda^{'}_j-i-j+1)$, and $\lambda'$ the partition conjugate to $\lambda$. Then $H_{\lambda}\ \mathrm{dim}\ \lambda=f_{\lambda}$, with $f_{\lambda}$ the dimension of the irreducible representation of the symmetric group associated to $\lambda$ (i.e. the number of standard tableaux of shape $\lambda$). Thus one recovers the classical distributions $$p_{\lambda}(\Lambda)= \frac{1}{|\Lambda|} \frac{f_{\Lambda}}{f_{\lambda}}\quad,\quad q_{\Lambda}(\lambda)= \frac{f_{\lambda}}{f_{\Lambda}}$$ Our results are new even in this classical case.

In it was shown that Young diagrams must be interpreted as a special case of “pairs of interlacing sequences”, and that transition and co-transition distributions can be defined in this more general frame. It is likely that our explicit evaluations can be easily translated in this context.

Rows and columns

To conclude we give the proof of two conjectures stated in Sections 9 and 10 of (all conjectures of these sections will then be established). This result was not included in, though it is a direct consequence of relation (5.1) proved there. We shall need the following lemma.

With $s(n,k)$ the Stirling numbers of the first kind, we have $$\frac{1}{x^k}=\sum_{n\ge k} s(n-1,k-1)\frac{1}{[x]_n}.$$

Let $\Delta$ be the finite difference operator defined by $\Delta f(y)=f(y+1)-f(y)$. We write the Newton interpolation formula $$f(y)=\sum_{n\ge 0}[y]_n \, \frac{\Delta^n f(0)}{n!},$$ for $f(y)=x/(x-y)=\sum_{r\ge 0} y^r/x^r$. This yields immediatly $$f(y)=\sum_{n\ge 0} [y]_n \, \frac{x}{[x]_{n+1}}.$$ Hence the result by identifying coefficients of $y^k$.

For any integer $p\ge 0$ we have $$\begin{split} {\binom{\lambda}{(p)}}_{\alpha} = \frac{1}{(1/\alpha)_p} \sum_{0 <i+j \le p} &\frac{1}{\alpha^i} \, s(p-1,i+j-1) \left(\sum_{k=0}^{min(i,j)}\binom{|\lambda|-j}{i-k}\,F_{jk}(\lambda) \right)\\ {\binom{\lambda}{1^p}}_{\alpha} = \frac{1}{(\alpha)_p} \sum_{0 <i+j \le p} (-1)^j& \alpha^{i+j} s(p-1,i+j-1) \left(\sum_{k=0}^{min(i,j)}\binom{|\lambda|-j}{i-k}\,F_{jk}(\lambda) \right). \end{split}$$

By the property of duality (, p. 320) $${\binom{\lambda}{(p)}}_{\alpha} ={\binom{\lambda'}{1^p}}_{1/\alpha}$$ and using $d_{k}(\lambda';1/\alpha)=(-\alpha)^k d_{k}(\lambda;\alpha)$, hence $F_{jk}(\lambda';1/\alpha)=(-\alpha)^j F_{jk}(\lambda;\alpha)$, it is enough to prove the second formula. The generalized Chu-Vandermonde formula proved in (Theorem 12.1, p. 161) reads $$\frac{(y+1)_{\lambda}}{(y)_{\lambda}} = \sum_{\mu} (-1)^{\mu} {\binom{\lambda}{\mu}}_{\alpha} \frac{(-1)_\mu}{(y)_\mu}= \sum_{p\ge 0} {\binom{\lambda}{1^p}}_{\alpha} \, \frac{(\alpha)_p}{[\alpha y]_p},$$ since $(-1)_\mu=0$ if $\mu_{1} > 1$. On the other hand relation (5.1) implies $$\frac{(y+1)_{\lambda}}{(y)_{\lambda}} = \sum_{i,j\ge 0} (-1)^{j} \frac{1}{y^{i+j}} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{min(i,j)}\binom{|\lambda|-j}{i-k}\,F_{jk}(\lambda) \right).$$ Using Lemma 11.1, we conclude by comparison.

How do the quantities $c_k(\lambda)$ and $C_k(\lambda)$ relate to classical Stirling numbers and what generating functions do they satisfy?

Based on the doc, the quantities $c_k(\lambda)$ and $C_k(\lambda)$ are generalizations of Stirling numbers of the first and second kind. Specifically:

- When $\lambda$ is a row partition $(n)$, $c_k(\lambda) = |s(n,k)|$, where $s(n,k)$ are the unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind. 

- When $\lambda$ is a row partition $(n)$, $C_k(\lambda) = S(n+k-1,n-1)$, where $S(n,k)$ are the Stirling numbers of the second kind.

They satisfy the following generating functions:

- $c_k(\lambda) = \sum_{|\mu|=k} (-1)^{k-l(\mu)} \frac{1}{z_\mu} d_\mu(\lambda)$

- $C_k(\lambda) = \sum_{|\mu|=k} \frac{1}{z_\mu} d_\mu(\lambda)$

Where $d_\mu(\lambda) = \prod_{i \ge 1} d_i(\lambda)^{m_i(\mu)}$ depends on the $\alpha$-contents of the cells of $\lambda$.

So in summary, $c_k(\lambda)$ and $C_k(\lambda)$ generalize Stirling numbers to partitions $\lambda$, with specific links to Stirling numbers when $\lambda$ is a row partition. Their generating functions relate them to the shifted symmetric functions $d_\mu(\lambda)$.

A train 1000 m long takes 15 sec to cross a man walking at 10 kmph in a direction opposite to that of the train on a gradual uphill incline of 5%. Considering the incline, the train's speed decreases by 10%. Find the original speed of the train before the incline.

First, let's convert the man's walking speed from kmph to m/s, because the train's crossing time is given in seconds.

Speed in m/s = Speed in kmph × (1000 m / 1 km) × (1 hour / 3600 seconds)
Speed of man in m/s = 10 × (1000 / 1) × (1 / 3600)
Speed of man in m/s = 10,000 / 3600
Speed of man in m/s = 100 / 36
Speed of man in m/s = 2.777... m/s

Now, let's find the relative speed between the train and the man. Since they are moving in opposite directions, we add their speeds to find the relative speed.

Let the original speed of the train be 'v' m/s. Due to the 5% uphill incline, the train's speed decreases by 10%. Therefore, the speed of the train on the incline is 90% of 'v', which is 0.9v m/s.

Relative speed = Speed of train on incline + Speed of man
Relative speed = 0.9v + 2.777...

The train takes 15 seconds to cross the man, and the length of the train is 1000 m. So, the relative speed can also be calculated by dividing the length of the train by the time taken to cross the man.

Relative speed = Length of train / Time taken to cross
Relative speed = 1000 m / 15 s
Relative speed = 66.666... m/s

Now, we can set up the equation with the relative speed:

0.9v + 2.777... = 66.666...
0.9v = 66.666... - 2.777...
0.9v = 63.888...

Now, we solve for 'v':

v = 63.888... / 0.9
v = 71.111... m/s

To find the original speed of the train before the incline, we convert 'v' back to kmph:

Speed in kmph = Speed in m/s × (1 km / 1000 m) × (3600 seconds / 1 hour)
Speed of train in kmph = 71.111... × (1 / 1000) × 3600
Speed of train in kmph = 71.111... × 3.6
Speed of train in kmph = 255.999... kmph

Therefore, the original speed of the train before the incline was approximately $\boxed{256}$  kmph.
Given the one-variable quadratic equation about $x$: $x^{2}-3x+1=0$ has two real roots $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$, then the value of $x_{1}+x_{2}-x_{1}x_{2}$ is ______.

Given the quadratic equation $x^{2}-3x+1=0$, we are asked to find the value of $x_{1}+x_{2}-x_{1}x_{2}$, where $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are the roots of the equation.

Step 1: Identify the coefficients of the quadratic equation, which are $a=1$, $b=-3$, and $c=1$.

Step 2: Use Vieta's formulas to find the sum and product of the roots. According to Vieta's formulas:
- The sum of the roots, $x_{1}+x_{2} = -\frac{b}{a}$
- The product of the roots, $x_{1}x_{2} = \frac{c}{a}$

Step 3: Calculate the sum of the roots:
\[x_{1}+x_{2} = -\frac{-3}{1} = 3\]

Step 4: Calculate the product of the roots:
\[x_{1}x_{2} = \frac{1}{1} = 1\]

Step 5: Find the value of $x_{1}+x_{2}-x_{1}x_{2}$:
\[x_{1}+x_{2}-x_{1}x_{2} = 3 - 1 = 2\]

Therefore, the value of $x_{1}+x_{2}-x_{1}x_{2}$ is $\boxed{2}$.

The area of the smallest square that can contain a circle of radius 6 is $\boxed{144}$.

I'm trying to understand a program called hexdump1 from the book "Assembly Language Step by Step 3rd edition". The program requires an argument in the form of "hexdump1 < input.txt". I'm using the EDB debugger and have set the application arguments as "< input.txt" and "input.txt". However, when I debug the code and reach the part where it reads input, the program runs through without allowing me to debug further. Is it not possible to debug an application with arguments using graphical debuggers? Is there a better graphical debugger that can help me with this?

The issue here is that the "< input.txt" part was not meant to be an argument for hexdump1. The program has been designed to read from the standard input and write to the standard output. The "< input.txt" part is actually a command line input that gets interpreted by the command interpreter (e.g., cmd.exe on Windows) to redirect the standard input stream of hexdump1 to read from the "input.txt" file.

When you launch hexdump1 from within the debugger, it does not interpret the "< input.txt" part as a redirection command. Instead, it passes it as a parameter to hexdump1, which ignores it and continues to read from the standard input. Since the standard input is empty in the debugger, hexdump1 does nothing.

Unfortunately, there is no direct solution to this problem. However, you can consider the following options:

1. Modify hexdump1 to accept a filename as a parameter and read from that file instead of relying on the standard input.

2. Explore the options of your debugger to see if there is a way to specify a file to redirect the standard input during debugging.

These are the general approaches you can take to overcome this issue. As for specific graphical debuggers, it would be best to research and try different ones to find the most suitable debugger for your needs.

A manufacturer of tennis balls claims that the mean weight of their tennis balls is 56 grams. You randomly select a sample of 25 tennis balls and find the mean weight to be 55 grams with a standard deviation of 2.5 grams. 

Assuming that the weights of the tennis balls follow a normal distribution, can you conclude, with a 95% level of confidence, that the mean weight of the tennis balls is different from the manufacturer's claim? Use hypothesis testing to support your conclusion.

To test the manufacturer's claim, we will perform a two-tailed hypothesis test. We will use the following null and alternative hypotheses:

Null hypothesis (H0): μ = 56 grams (the mean weight of the tennis balls is equal to the manufacturer's claim)
Alternative hypothesis (H1): μ ≠ 56 grams (the mean weight of the tennis balls is different from the manufacturer's claim)

We are given the following information:
Sample mean (x̄) = 55 grams
Sample size (n) = 25 tennis balls
Sample standard deviation (s) = 2.5 grams
Significance level (α) = 0.05 (for a 95% confidence level)

First, we need to calculate the standard error (SE) of the sample mean:
SE = s / √n = 2.5 / √25 = 2.5 / 5 = 0.5 grams

Next, we will calculate the test statistic (t-score) using the following formula:
t = (x̄ - μ) / SE = (55 - 56) / 0.5 = -1 / 0.5 = -2

Now, we need to find the critical t-value for a two-tailed test with a 95% confidence level and 24 degrees of freedom (n - 1 = 25 - 1 = 24). Using a t-distribution table or calculator, we find the critical t-value to be approximately ±2.064.

Since our calculated t-score (-2) falls within the range of the critical t-values (-2.064 to 2.064), we fail to reject the null hypothesis. This means that, with a 95% level of confidence, we cannot conclude that the mean weight of the tennis balls is different from the manufacturer's claim of 56 grams.

Mary and Harry enter into a partnership by investing $700 and $300 respectively. At the end of one year, they divided their profits such that some portion of the profit is divided equally for the efforts they have put into the business and the remaining amount of profit is divided in the ratio of the investments they made in the business. Mary received $800 more than Harry did. The profit made by their business in that year was $3000. What portion of the profit was divided equally for their efforts?

Let's denote the total profit by P, which is given as $3000.

Let's denote the portion of the profit that is divided equally for their efforts as E.

The remaining profit, which is P - E, is divided in the ratio of their investments, which is 7:3 (since Mary invested $700 and Harry invested $300).

Mary's share of the remaining profit is \(\frac{7}{7+3}\) (P - E) = \(\frac{7}{10}\) (P - E).

Harry's share of the remaining profit is \(\frac{3}{7+3}\) (P - E) = \(\frac{3}{10}\) (P - E).

Mary's total share is E/2 + \(\frac{7}{10}\) (P - E).

Harry's total share is E/2 + \(\frac{3}{10}\) (P - E).

It is given that Mary received $800 more than Harry did, so:

Mary's total share - Harry's total share = $800

(E/2 + \(\frac{7}{10}\) (P - E)) - (E/2 + \(\frac{3}{10}\) (P - E)) = $800

Simplifying the equation:

E/2 + \(\frac{7}{10}\) P - \(\frac{7}{10}\) E - E/2 - \(\frac{3}{10}\) P + \(\frac{3}{10}\) E = $800

Combining like terms:

\(\frac{7}{10}\) P - \(\frac{7}{10}\) E - \(\frac{3}{10}\) P + \(\frac{3}{10}\) E = $800

\(\frac{4}{10}\) P - \(\frac{4}{10}\) E = $800

\(\frac{4}{10}\) (P - E) = $800

Now, we know that P = $3000, so we can substitute that into the equation:

\(\frac{4}{10}\) ($3000 - E) = $800

$1200 - \(\frac{4}{10}\) E = $800

Subtract $1200 from both sides:

- \(\frac{4}{10}\) E = $800 - $1200

- \(\frac{4}{10}\) E = -$400

Now, divide both sides by - \(\frac{4}{10}\) to solve for E:

E = -$400 / - \(\frac{4}{10}\)

E = $1000

So, the portion of the profit that was divided equally for their efforts is $\boxed{\$1000}$ .

So, the total cost for 2 bottles is $20.00 x 2 = $40.00.
To find the cost per load of laundry in cents, we need to divide the total cost by the number of loads.

The answer is: 25

Given that $\theta$ is an angle in the fourth quadrant and $\sin(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4}) = \frac{3}{5}$, find $\tan(\theta - \frac{\pi}{4}) = \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.$

From the given information, we know that $\sin(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4}) = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\theta$ is in the fourth quadrant.

Since $\theta$ is in the fourth quadrant, we know that $\cos(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4}) > 0$.

Thus, we can find $\cos(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})$ using the Pythagorean identity:
$$\cos(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4}) = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})} = \frac{4}{5}.$$

Now, let's find $\tan(\theta - \frac{\pi}{4})$:
$$
\begin{align}
\tan(\theta - \frac{\pi}{4}) &= \tan(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{\pi}{2}) \\
&= -\frac{\sin[\frac{\pi}{2} - (\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})]}{\cos[\frac{\pi}{2} - (\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})]} \\
&= -\frac{\cos(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})}{\sin(\theta + \frac{\pi}{4})} \\
&= -\frac{4}{5} \times \frac{5}{3} \\
&= \boxed{-\frac{4}{3}}.
\end{align}
$$

What is the diameter of the circle inscribed in triangle $PQR$ if $PQ = 13$, $PR = 14$, and $QR = 15$?

Let $d$ be the diameter of the inscribed circle and $r$ the radius. Let $s$ be the semiperimeter of the triangle, calculated as $s = \frac{PQ + PR + QR}{2} = \frac{13 + 14 + 15}{2} = 21$.

Using Heron's formula to find the area of $\triangle PQR$:
\[
K = \sqrt{s(s-PQ)(s-PR)(s-QR)} = \sqrt{21 \cdot (21-13) \cdot (21-14) \cdot (21-15)} = \sqrt{21 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6}.
\]
Simplifying this product,
\[
K = \sqrt{21 \cdot 8 \cdot 7 \cdot 6} = \sqrt{21 \cdot 336} = \sqrt{7056},
\]
since $\sqrt{7056} = 84$ (by calculation $6 \times 14 = 84$).

Using the relationship of the area with the radius and semiperimeter, $K = rs$, we get
\[
84 = r \cdot 21.
\]
Thus,
\[
r = \frac{84}{21} = 4.
\]
Therefore, the diameter $d$ is $2r = 2 \times 4 = \boxed{8}$.

Let $Q$ be a plane passing through the origin. When $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ is projected onto plane $Q,$ the result is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.$ When $\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ is projected onto plane $Q,$ what is the result?

The vector from $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ to $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} 3-1 \\ 4-2 \\ 2-1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Scaling, we can take $\mathbf{n} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ as the normal vector of plane $Q.$ Thus, the equation of plane $Q$ is:
\[ 2x + 2y + z = 0. \]

Now, let $\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}$ and let $\mathbf{p}$ be its projection onto plane $Q.$ We know $\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{n}$. Hence, 
\[
\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{p} = \frac{\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}}{\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}} \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
= \frac{18}{9} \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then,
\[
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{v} - \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \boxed{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -3 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}}.
\]

Let \( P \) be a point inside triangle \( ABC \) such that
\[ 2\overrightarrow{PA} + 3\overrightarrow{PB} + \overrightarrow{PC} = \mathbf{0}. \]
Find the ratio of the area of triangle \( ABC \) to the area of triangle \( APB \).

We let \( \mathbf{a} = \overrightarrow{A}, \mathbf{b} = \overrightarrow{B}, \mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{C} \), and \( \mathbf{p} = \overrightarrow{P} \). Then the equation \( 2\overrightarrow{PA} + 3\overrightarrow{PB} + \overrightarrow{PC} = \mathbf{0} \) becomes
\[ 2(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{p}) + 3(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{p}) + (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{0}. \]
This simplifies to
\[ 2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} - 6\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{0}, \]
so solving for \( \mathbf{p} \), we find
\[ \mathbf{p} = \frac{2\mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}}{6}. \]

Let \( E \) be the intersection of \( AP \) and \( BC \):
\[ \mathbf{e} = \frac{2}{6} \mathbf{a} + \frac{3}{6} \mathbf{b} + \frac{1}{6} \mathbf{c} \]
since \( AP:PE = 5:1 \) by the mass points method (adding coefficients of \( a, b, c \)).

Triangles \( ABE \) and \( APE \) have the same height with respect to base \( \overline{BE} \), so their area ratio is equal to the ratio of their bases:
\[ \frac{[ABE]}{[APE]} = \frac{BE}{PE} = 5. \]
Similarly, triangles \( BCE \) and \( BPE \) have the same height with respect to base \( \overline{BE} \), so
\[ \frac{[BCE]}{[BPE]} = \frac{BE}{PE} = 5. \]
Therefore,
\[ \frac{[ABC]}{[APB]} = \frac{[ABE] + [BCE]}{[APE] + [BPE]} = \boxed{5}. \]

Three fair, standard six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the numbers on the top faces is 3? Express your answer as a common fraction.

For the sum of the numbers on the top faces of three dice to be 3, each die must show a 1. Since each die is six-sided and fair, the probability of rolling a 1 on any single die is $\frac{1}{6}$. Because the dice rolls are independent:
- Probability of the first die showing 1 is $\frac{1}{6}$.
- Probability of the second die showing 1 is $\frac{1}{6}$.
- Probability of the third die showing 1 is $\frac{1}{6}$.

The combined probability of all three dice showing 1 is:
\[
\frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{216}
\]

Thus, the probability that the sum of the numbers on the top faces is 3 is $\boxed{\frac{1}{216}}$.

Calculate the sum $1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + 19 + 21$.

This arithmetic series 1, 3, 5, ..., 19, 21, has a common difference of 2, just like the original series. To find the $n^{\text{th}}$ term formula, it is $1 + 2(n - 1) = 2n - 1$. If $2n - 1 = 21$, then solving for $n$ gives us $n = 11$. Hence, the series has 11 terms.

The sum of an arithmetic series can be calculated using the formula:
\[
\text{Sum} = \frac{\text{First term} + \text{Last term}}{2} \times \text{Number of terms}
\]
Plugging in the values, we get:
\[
\text{Sum} = \frac{1 + 21}{2} \times 11 = 11 \times 11 = 121
\]
Thus, the sum of the series $1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + 19 + 21$ is $\boxed{121}$.

11: $11$
12: $2^2\cdot3$
Then, we take the highest power of each prime that appears in the prime factorization:
$2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11=660$

Total = Band + Sports - Both

- Total is the total number of students involved in either band or sports (225 students).
- Band is the number of students in the band (85 students).
- Sports is the number of students on sports teams (200 students).
- Both is the number of students involved in both activities.

The sum of an arithmetic series is equal to the average of the first and last term, multiplied by the number of terms, so the sum is $\frac{(0+b-1)(b)}{2}=\frac{(b-1)(b)}{2}$.
Since the sum is $34_b$, we have $\frac{(b-1)(b)}{2}=34_b$.
We can convert $34_b$ to base 10 using the definition of base $b$ notation: $34_b=3b+4$.
So we have $\frac{(b-1)(b)}{2}=3b+4$.
Multiplying both sides by 2 gives $(b-1)(b)=6b+8$.
Expanding gives $b^2-b=6b+8$.
Rearranging and simplifying gives $b^2-7b-8=0$.
Factoring gives $(b-8)(b+1)=0$.
Since $b$ must be a positive integer, we have $b=\boxed{8}$.
The answer is: 8

If Jane had a 500-page book to read and she read the first half at a speed of 10 pages per day, and the second half at a speed of 5 pages per day, how many days did it take her to finish reading the book?

The book has 500 pages in total.
Jane read the first half, which is 500/2 = 250 pages, at a speed of 10 pages per day.
It took her 250/10 = 25 days to finish the first half.
She then read the second half, which is also 250 pages, at a speed of 5 pages per day.
It took her 250/5 = 50 days to finish the second half.
Therefore, it took Jane a total of 25 + 50 = 75 days to finish reading the book.
#### 75
The answer is: 75

Given a ten-sided regular polygon $B_1B_2B_3B_4B_5B_6B_7B_8B_9B_{10}$, how many distinct equilateral triangles in the plane of the polygon have at least two vertices in the set $\{B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_{10}\}$?

- We begin by calculating how many equilateral triangles can potentially be formed by selecting any two vertices from the decagon. Each pair of vertices uniquely determines one equilateral triangle, so we need to count the total number of distinct pairs of vertices. This is given by the combination formula $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ pairs. Each pair allows for two possible equilateral triangles (one to the left and one to the right of the line segment joining the pair), resulting in $45 \times 2 = 90$ potential triangles.
- Next, we need to account for overcounting. In a regular decagon, there exists equilateral triangles that are formed by vertices that are spaced four vertices apart (e.g., $B_1B_5B_9$). There are 10 such triangles, one starting from each vertex.
- To find overcounting, these triangles are counted four times each, once for each pair of their vertices. Therefore, we have $10 \times 3 = 30$ counts of these triangles, but we should only count them once. Thus, we have overcounted 20 times.
- Subtracting the overcounted triangles, we have $90 - 20 = 70$ distinct equilateral triangles.

$\boxed{70}$ distinct equilateral triangles.
In how many ways can 6 distinct beads be placed on a bracelet? (Note that two arrangements are the same if one can be rotated or reflected to produce the other.)

First, we place one bead on the bracelet. It doesn't matter where we place it since we can rotate the bracelet to any position.
Next, we place the remaining 5 beads one by one. Again, it doesn't matter where we place each bead initially since we can rotate the bracelet to any position.
However, we need to account for reflections. If we have placed the first 3 beads in a clockwise order, then there are 3 possible reflections: one where all beads are flipped, one where the first and third bead are flipped, and one where the second and third bead are flipped.
Therefore, the number of distinct arrangements is $\frac{6!}{6 \cdot 2} = \frac{720}{12} = \boxed{60}$.
The answer is: 60

Determine if Rolle's theorem applies to the function \( f(x) = x^2 + 2x + 7 \) on the interval \([-6, 4]\), and if so, find the corresponding value \( c \).

1. **Verification of continuity and differentiability**:
   \[
   f(x) = x^2 + 2x + 7
   \]
   The function \( f(x) \) is a polynomial, and since all polynomials are continuous and differentiable everywhere on the real line, \( f(x) \) is continuous and differentiable on the interval \([-6, 4]\).

2. **Evaluate the function at the endpoints**:
   Calculate \( f(-6) \):
   \[
   f(-6) = (-6)^2 + 2(-6) + 7 = 36 - 12 + 7 = 31
   \]
   Calculate \( f(4) \):
   \[
   f(4) = 4^2 + 2(4) + 7 = 16 + 8 + 7 = 31
   \]
   Since \( f(-6) = f(4) = 31 \), the function satisfies the condition \( f(a) = f(b) \) for \( a = -6 \) and \( b = 4 \).

3. **Find the derivative**:
   \[
   f'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(x^2 + 2x + 7) = 2x + 2
   \]

4. **Find the critical points in the open interval \((-6, 4)\)**:
   Set the derivative equal to zero and solve for \( x \):
   \[
   2x + 2 = 0
   \]
   \[
   2x = -2
   \]
   \[
   x = -1
   \]

5. **Verification that the critical point is within the interval**:
   The value \( x = -1 \) lies within the open interval \((-6, 4)\).

### Conclusion:
The function \( f(x) = x^2 + 2x + 7 \) satisfies all the conditions of Rolle's theorem on the interval \([-6, 4]\). The corresponding value of \( c \) in the interval \((-6, 4)\) is:
\[
\boxed{-1}
\]
Determine the smallest value of $y$ that satisfies the equation $|y - 8| = 15$.

We start by interpreting the equation $|y - 8| = 15$. This can be broken down into two cases:
1. $y - 8 = 15$
2. $y - 8 = -15$

Solving each case:
1. $y - 8 = 15 \implies y = 15 + 8 = 23$
2. $y - 8 = -15 \implies y = -15 + 8 = -7$

Thus, the solutions for $y$ are $y = 23$ and $y = -7$. Since the problem asks for the smallest value of $y$, the solution is $\boxed{-7}$.
Find the product of the values of \( x \) that satisfy the equation \( |2x - 1| + 4 = 24 \).

1. **Isolate the absolute value expression**:
   \[
   |2x - 1| + 4 = 24 \quad \Rightarrow \quad |2x - 1| = 24 - 4 = 20
   \]
   
2. **Consider both cases of the absolute value**:
   - When \( 2x - 1 = 20 \):
     \[
     2x = 20 + 1 = 21 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = \frac{21}{2} = 10.5
     \]
   - When \( 2x - 1 = -20 \):
     \[
     2x = -20 + 1 = -19 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x = \frac{-19}{2} = -9.5
     \]
   
3. **Find the product of the solutions**:
   \[
   (10.5) \times (-9.5) = -99.75
   \]

Conclusion:
The product of the values of \( x \) that satisfy the equation is \(\boxed{-99.75}\).

A bored student walks down a hall that contains a row of closed lockers, numbered $1$ to $1024$. He opens the locker numbered 1, and then alternates between skipping and opening each locker thereafter. When he reaches the end of the hall, the student turns around and starts back. He opens the first closed locker he encounters, and then alternates between skipping and opening each closed locker thereafter. The student continues wandering back and forth in this manner until every locker is open. What is the number of the last locker he opens?

To understand the process of opening the lockers, we'll follow the student's actions step by step, closely adhering to the solution provided.

1. **First Pass:** The student opens all odd-numbered lockers. This means every locker numbered $1, 3, 5, \ldots, 1023$ is opened. The remaining closed lockers are all even, i.e., $2, 4, 6, \ldots, 1024$.

2. **Second Pass:** The student then opens lockers that are multiples of $4$, leaving only lockers that are $2 \pmod{8}$ and $6 \pmod{8}$ closed. This means lockers like $2, 6, 10, 14, \ldots$ remain closed.

3. **Subsequent Passes:** The pattern continues as follows:
   - Opens all lockers $2 \pmod{8}$, leaving $6 \pmod{16}$ and $14 \pmod{16}$ closed.
   - Opens all lockers $14 \pmod{16}$, leaving $6 \pmod{32}$ and $22 \pmod{32}$ closed.
   - Opens all lockers $6 \pmod{32}$, leaving $22 \pmod{64}$ and $54 \pmod{64}$ closed.
   - Opens all lockers $54 \pmod{64}$, leaving $22 \pmod{128}$ and $86 \pmod{128}$ closed.
   - Opens all lockers $22 \pmod{128}$, leaving $86 \pmod{256}$ and $214 \pmod{256}$ closed.
   - Opens all lockers $214 \pmod{256}$, leaving $86 \pmod{512}$ and $342 \pmod{512}$ closed.
   - Finally, the student is left with lockers $86, 342, 598$, and $854$.

4. **Last Passes:** The student opens locker $86$ and $598$ on his way, and then opens locker $854$ on his way back, leaving locker number $342$ as the last closed locker.

Therefore, the last locker the student opens is $\boxed{342}$.

Implement a Python function `find_first_place` that takes a list of dictionaries `data` representing soccer players and returns the player with the highest `rating`. Use list comprehension to create a new list containing only the players with the highest rating. If there are multiple players with the same highest rating, return the one with the lowest `id`. Handle the case where the input list is empty.

Here's the code in Python to achieve the desired functionality:

```python
def find_first_place(data):
    if not data:
        return None

    highest_rating = max(player['rating'] for player in data)
    players_with_highest_rating = [player for player in data if player['rating'] == highest_rating]
    players_with_highest_rating.sort(key=lambda player: player['id'])

    return players_with_highest_rating[0]
```

In an effort to replace my home backup server with Amazon's S3, I've been collecting a list of Amazon S3 compatible backup tools to look at. Here's what I've discovered, followed by my requirements.
I've evaluated exactly zero of these so far. That's next.
s3sync.rb is written in Ruby as a sort of rsync clone to replace the perl script s3sync which is now abandonware. Given that I already use rsync for much of my backup system, this is highly appealing.
Backup Manager appears to now have S3 support as of version 0.7.3. It's a command-line tool for Linux (and likely other Unix-like systems).
s3DAV isn't exactly a backup tool. It's provides a WebDAV front-end (or "virtual filesystem") to S3 storage, so you could use many other backup tools with S3. Recent versions of Windows and Mac OS have WebDAV support built-in. Java is required for s3DAV.
S3 Backup is an Open Source tool for backing up to S3. It's currently available only for Windows. Mac and Linux versions appear to be planned. The UI is built on wxWidgets.
duplicity is a free Unix tool that uses S3 and the librsync library. It is written in Python but not considered suitable for backing up important data quite yet.
S3 Solutions is a list of other S3 related tools on the Amazon Developer Connection.
Brackup is a backup tool written by Brad Fitzpatrick (of LiveJournal, SixApart, memcached, perlbal, etc...). It's written in Perl, fairly new, and doesn't have a lot in the way of documentation yet.
Jungle Disk provides clients for Mac, Windows, and Linux. It also offers a local WebDAV server.
DragonDisk has Linux and Windows clients.
For those keeping track, non-S3 options suggested in the comment on my previous post are Carbonite, rsync.net, and a DreamHost account.
Are there other S3 tools that I'm missing?
Also, I've found that Amazon's S3 forum is quite helpful. The discussion there is generally of good quality and the software does the job nicely. Perhaps we should do something similar for YDN instead of using Yahoo! Groups?

I’ve been thinking of using S3 to store backups of various machines (basically all linux/OSX ones), but what’s been holding me back is the inability of S3 to do rsync on the server side. rsync really needs an instance of rsync running “near” where the data is stored in order to do its cleverest compression/do-not-transmit smarts. Rsync is basically a win if you have a high-bandwidth link between the rsync server and the backing store, and a lower bandwidth link between the rsync server and client. With S3, you’d have to run the rsync server side yourself, remote from S3, which kind of defeats the purpose of rsync… But then I had a brainstorm.
Amazon’s ECC service, which parallels S3, allows you to create a virtual machine and turn it on/off as needed in the amazon compute cloud. The ECC instances have high-bandwidth connectivity to S3 storage, and so would be ideal for running an rsync server! You can set up an ECC instance which serves rsync, and then your backup script can turn the instance on, do the rsync, then shut the instance down when it’s done.
Now all I have to do is actually create the ECC instance, then create some kind of wrapper around the whole thing which does the startup-backup-shutdown wrapping around the ECC API, and voila!
How much upstream bandwidth do you have to make this satisfactory? My measly 512K upstream makes backing up online sound like a drag (though I do do appreciate the reliability and general peace-of-mind).
As much as I'm willing to pay for. Again, I'm mainly backing up data that's already hosted in a data center somewhere.
