We have presented here a teaching that Rabbi Seidenberg shared over the neoḥasid announcement listserve, “Chasidus w/o Borders” in 2013 just prior to the book entering its final phase of editing. Additionally, I have included with his teaching the sourcetexts he referenced from the Talmud Bavli, tractate Brakhot, and Rabbi Moshe Cordovero’s Palm Tree of Devorah. –Aharon N. Varady, ed.
The Talmud (Brakhot 35a-b, see below) teaches that eating food without saying a brakhah (a blessing) beforehand is like stealing. A lot of people know that teaching, and it’s pretty deep. But here’s an even deeper part: the Talmud doesn’t call it “stealing”, but מעילה (“me’ilah“), which means taking from sacred property that belongs to the Temple. So that means that everything in the world is sacred and this Creation is like a HOLY TEMPLE.
If me’ilah means that you can’t use property that’s sanctified, that’s because sanctified property must be used for a sacred purpose and it must be used by the priests. So if saying a brakhah changes the status of something so that you can now eat it, what status is the brakhah changing? Is it turning the food into something that’s no longer sacred and can therefore be used by an ordinary person (a הֶדיוֹט “hedyot“)? OR, is it turning the person from a hedyot into a priest?
I think it means that by saying a blessing before we eat–or before we take in any pleasure that has a brakhah–we become like priests administering to Creation, which means we take on an awesome responsibility: that we should act not just for our own sake but for the sake of all people and all beings. That’s the role of the priest in the Temple.
I bless us that we all merit to really see the world through such eyes, and that our every act of eating, of taking, from this world, be an act of sanctification and blessing — meaning, not just blessing God, but bringing blessing, to all the creatures that we share this planet with. Or, in Rabbi Moshe Cordovero‘s words, זֶה הַכְּלָל, הַחֶמְלָה עַל כָּל הַנִּמְצָאִים שֶׁלֹּא לְחַבְּלָם, תְּלוּיָה בְּחָכְמָה — may we live and work and act so that our actions “cause life to stream forth, to all beings”.

GEMARAH […] Our Rabbis have taught: A person is forbidden to enjoy anything of this world without a blessing, and whoever does so commits sacrilege. What is the remedy? Let them go to a Sage. Let them go to a Sage! What can they do for them, seeing that they have done what is forbidden? But, said Rava: [The meaning is,] let them from the first go to a Sage who will teach them the blessings, so that they should not come to commit sacrilege.
Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel: Whoever enjoys anything of this world without a blessing is as though he had partaken of the holy things of Heaven; as it is said, “The Earth is for YHVH and the fullness thereof” (Psalms 24:1). Rav Levi asked: It is written, “The Earth is for YHVH and the fullness thereof,” and it is written, “The heavens are the heavens of YHVH, but the Earth he has given to the children of Adam” (Psalms 115:16)! There is no contradiction; the former passage referring [[fol. 35 b.]] to before the blessing [has been uttered], the latter to after the blessing. Rav Ḥannina bar Pappa said: Whoever enjoys anything of this world without a blessing is as though he robbed the blessed Holy One and the Community of Israel; as it is said, “Whoso robs his father or his mother and says, It is no transgression, the same is the companion of a destroyer” (Proverbs 28:24) — “father” is none other than the blessed Holy One; as it is said, “Is not He your father that has acquired you?” (Deut. 32:6); and “mother” is none other than the Community of Israel; as it is said, “Hear, my son, the instruction of your father, and forsake not the teaching of your mother” (Proverbs 1:8). What means “the companion of a destroyer”? Rav Ḥannina bar Pappa said: He is the companion of Yerovam the son of Nevat, who corrupted Yisrael against their Father in Heaven.

Now to the Supernal attribute of Ḥokhmah, there are two aspects. The higher aspect – which faces Keter and does not face downwards; rather, it receives from above. The second and lower aspect – faces downwards, overseeing the other sefirot, to which it extends its Ḥokhmah. Likewise a person should have two aspects: The first aspect should be his contemplation in solitude with his Creator in order to increase and perfect his Ḥokhmah; the second should be to teach others the Ḥokhmah that the blessed Holy One has bestowed upon him. And just as the Supernal attribute of Ḥokhmah bestows to each sefirah according to its measure and needs, so, too, one should bestow his Ḥokhmah to each person according to the measure his intellect can bear, and to what is proper for him and his needs. One should be careful not to give more than the mind of the recipient can contain, so that no harm will result, just as the Supernal sefirah of Ḥokhmah does not add on more than the limited capacity of the recipient (sefirah).

A man can swim in still water at 9 km/h. He takes a certain amount of time to swim upstream and downstream. The speed of the stream is 3 km/h. What is the ratio of the time taken to swim upstream to the time taken to swim downstream?

When the man swims upstream, the speed of the stream works against him, so his effective speed is reduced. When he swims downstream, the speed of the stream works with him, so his effective speed is increased.

The man's speed in still water is 9 km/h, and the speed of the stream is 3 km/h.

When swimming upstream, his effective speed is:
Speed upstream = Speed in still water - Speed of stream
Speed upstream = 9 km/h - 3 km/h
Speed upstream = 6 km/h

When swimming downstream, his effective speed is:
Speed downstream = Speed in still water + Speed of stream
Speed downstream = 9 km/h + 3 km/h
Speed downstream = 12 km/h

Let's assume the man swims a distance of D km both upstream and downstream.

The time taken to swim upstream is:
Time upstream = Distance / Speed upstream
Time upstream = D / 6

The time taken to swim downstream is:
Time downstream = Distance / Speed downstream
Time downstream = D / 12

Now, we can find the ratio of the time taken to swim upstream to the time taken to swim downstream:
Ratio = Time upstream / Time downstream
Ratio = (D / 6) / (D / 12)
Ratio = (D / 6) * (12 / D)
Ratio = 12 / 6
Ratio = 2 / 1

Therefore, the ratio of the time taken to swim upstream to the time taken to swim downstream is $\boxed{2:1}$ .

Since $\overrightarrow {a}$ and $\overrightarrow {b}$ are both unit vectors with an angle of 120° between them, we have:

$\overrightarrow {a} \cdot \overrightarrow {b} = 1 \times 1 \times \cos{120°} = -\frac{1}{2}$

Then, we can calculate the magnitude of $\overrightarrow {a} + 2 \overrightarrow {b}$ as follows:

$|\overrightarrow {a} + 2 \overrightarrow {b}|^2 = (\overrightarrow {a} + 2 \overrightarrow {b}) \cdot (\overrightarrow {a} + 2 \overrightarrow {b}) = \overrightarrow {a} \cdot \overrightarrow {a} + 4 \overrightarrow {a} \cdot \overrightarrow {b} + 4 \overrightarrow {b} \cdot \overrightarrow {b} = 1 + 4 \times (-\frac{1}{2}) + 4 = 3$

Therefore, $|\overrightarrow {a} + 2 \overrightarrow {b}| = \sqrt{3}$.

$(2)$ If the equation has one root greater than $0$, find the range of values for $k$.

### Problem:

For the one-variable quadratic equation $x^{2}-kx-k-1=0$.

#### Part 1: Prove that the equation always has two real roots.

#### Part 2: If the equation has one root greater than $0$, find the range of values for $k$.

### Solution:

#### Part 1: Proof that the equation always has two real roots.

To determine the nature of the roots of a quadratic equation, we can use the discriminant, $\Delta$, which is given by $\Delta = b^{2} - 4ac$ for a quadratic equation of the form $ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$.

Given the equation $x^{2}-kx-k-1=0$, we identify $a=1$, $b=-k$, and $c=-k-1$. Substituting these values into the formula for the discriminant, we get:

\[
\Delta = (-k)^{2} - 4(1)(-k-1) = k^{2} + 4k + 4
\]

This can be further simplified to:

\[
\Delta = (k + 2)^{2}
\]

Since the square of any real number is always non-negative, we have:

\[
\Delta = (k + 2)^{2} \geqslant 0
\]

This proves that the discriminant is always non-negative, which means the quadratic equation always has two real roots (either distinct or equal). Therefore, we have proven that the equation always has two real roots.

#### Part 2: Finding the range of values for $k$ when one root is greater than $0$.

Given the equation $x^{2}-kx-k-1=0$, we can factor it as follows:

\[
x^{2}-kx-k-1 = (x - (k+1))(x + 1) = 0
\]

This gives us the roots of the equation as:

\[
x = k + 1 \quad \text{or} \quad x = -1
\]

For the equation to have one root greater than $0$, the root $x = k + 1$ must be greater than $0$. Therefore, we have:

\[
k + 1 > 0 \implies k > -1
\]

Thus, for the equation to have one root greater than $0$, the value of $k$ must be greater than $-1$. Therefore, the range of values for $k$ is:

\[

(d) Prove that 3999991 is not a prime number.

   - To factor $x^{2} - 4$ as the product of two linear expressions in $x$:
   - Recognize that $x^{2} - 4$ can be rewritten as a difference of squares: $(x)^{2} - (2)^{2}$.
   - Apply the difference of squares formula: $a^{2} - b^{2} = (a - b)(a + b)$.
   - Using $a = x$ and $b = 2$:
     $$x^{2} - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)$$

   Conclusion:

   - Factor out the 100 to find $k$:
     $$98^{2} - 4 = 100 \cdot 96$$

   $$k = 96.$$

   - Set $a = 20$ and $b = n$:
     $$20^2 - n^2 = 391$$
   - Calculate the left side:
     $$400 - n^2 = 391$$
     $$400 - 391 = n^2$$
     $$n^2 = 9$$
   - Take the square root of both sides:
     $$n = \pm 3$$
   - Since $n$ is a positive integer:
     $$n = 3$$
   - Verify:
     $$20 - n = 17 \quad \text{and} \quad 20 + n = 23$$
     $$17 \cdot 23 = 391$$

   Conclusion:
   $$\boxed{3}$$

   - We need to determine if 3999991 is a prime number by factoring it.

The equilateral triangle \(PQR\) has side length 1. The lines \(PT\) and \(PU\) trisect the angle \(RPQ\), the lines \(RS\) and \(RT\) trisect the angle \(QRP\), and the lines \(QS\) and \(QU\) trisect the angle \(PQR\). What is the side length of the equilateral triangle \(STU\)?

A) \(\frac{\cos 80^{\circ}}{\cos 20^{\circ}}\)

B) \(\frac{1}{3} \cos 20^{\circ}\)

C) \(\cos ^{2} 20^{\circ}\)

D) \(\frac{1}{6}\)

E) \(\cos 20^{\circ} \cos 80^{\circ}\)

1. **Identify the primary setup**: The given triangle \( PQR \) is equilateral with each side of length 1. Therefore, each interior angle of \( PQR \) is \( 60^\circ \).

2. **Angle trisection**: The lines \( PT \) and \( PU \) trisect \( \angle RPQ \), which means both \( \angle QPU \) and \( \angle UPT \) are \( 20^\circ \).

3. **Symmetry consideration**: Due to the symmetry, \( QU = PU = PT \).

4. **Determine length \( PU \)**: 
   - In triangle \( PQ U \), let \( X \) be the perpendicular from \( U \) to \( PQ \). 
   - Since \( \angle QPU = 20^\circ \), in \( \triangle PXU \), \( \angle XPU = 20^\circ \).
   - The relation \( \cos 20^\circ = \frac{PX}{PU} \). 
   - Now, \( PX = \frac{1}{2} \) (as \( PX \) is the half of \( PQ \)), so:
     \[
     \cos 20^\circ = \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{PU} \implies PU = \frac{\frac{1}{2}}{\cos 20^\circ} = \frac{1}{2 \cos 20^\circ}
     \]

5. **Calculate length \( UT \)**:
   - In \( \triangle PYU \), let \( Y \) be the perpendicular from \( P \) to \( UT \).
   - \( \angle UYP = 80^\circ \) (as \( \angle UPY = 10^\circ \) and the sum with \( 90^\circ \)).
   - Taking \( PU \) from above,
     \[
     \cos 80^\circ = \frac{UY}{PU} \implies UY = PU \cos 80^\circ = \left(\frac{1}{2 \cos 20^\circ}\right) \cos 80^\circ = \frac{\cos 80^\circ}{2 \cos 20^\circ}
     \]
   - Since \( UY \) is half of \( UT \):
     \[
     UT = 2 \times UY = \frac{\cos 80^\circ}{\cos 20^\circ}
     \]

6. **Conclusion**: The side length of the equilateral triangle \( STU \) is:
   \[
   \boxed{\frac{\cos 80^\circ}{\cos 20^\circ}}
   \]

How does Python compare strings? Specifically, how does Python determine the outcome when a less than < or greater than > operator is used? For example, when I execute print('abc' < 'bac'), it returns True. I understand that this is because it compares corresponding characters in the string, however it's unclear why the comparison gives more weight to the fact that a is less than b (in first position) in the first string rather than the fact that a is less than b in the second string (in second position). Could you please explain this?

Python string comparisons are done lexicographically i.e., using ASCII value of the characters. This is very similar to how words are sorted in a dictionary where the alphabetical order of characters is considered. When Python compares two strings, it compares characters by characters. If the first character from the first string is less (has less ASCII value) than the first character from the second string, then the first string is considered less than the second string regardless of the other characters present in the strings. This is illustrated in your example print('abc' < 'bac'). Here 'abc' is considered less than 'bac' because the first character 'a' in 'abc' has less ASCII value than the first character 'b' in 'bac'. The other characters are not even considered in this comparison. So the "weight" you are referring to is actually the position of the characters in the string. The characters at the beginning of the string have more "weight" because they are considered first in the comparison. This is why 'a' being less than 'b' at the first position is more significant than 'a' being less than 'b' at the second position.

If the one-variable quadratic equation $kx^{2}-2x-1=0$ has two distinct real roots with respect to $x$, then the range of real number $k$ is ( )

A: $k \gt -1$

B: $k \lt 1$ and $k\neq 0$

C: $k\geqslant -1$ and $k\neq 0$

D: $k \gt -1$ and $k\neq 0$

To determine the range of the real number $k$ for which the quadratic equation $kx^{2}-2x-1=0$ has two distinct real roots, we need to analyze the discriminant $\Delta$ of the equation. The discriminant $\Delta$ is given by the formula $\Delta = b^{2} - 4ac$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are the coefficients of $x^{2}$, $x$, and the constant term, respectively, in the quadratic equation $ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$.

Given the equation $kx^{2}-2x-1=0$, we have $a = k$, $b = -2$, and $c = -1$. Substituting these values into the discriminant formula gives us:
\[
\Delta = (-2)^{2} - 4(k)(-1) = 4 + 4k.
\]

For the equation to have two distinct real roots, the discriminant $\Delta$ must be greater than 0. Therefore, we set up the inequality:
\[
4 + 4k > 0.
\]

Solving this inequality for $k$ gives us:
\[
4k > -4 \implies k > -1.
\]

However, we must also consider that for a quadratic equation $ax^{2} + bx + c = 0$ to be valid, $a \neq 0$. In this case, $a = k$, so we must have $k \neq 0$.

Combining these two conditions, we find that $k$ must be greater than $-1$ and not equal to $0$. Therefore, the correct range of $k$ is:
\[
k > -1 \quad \text{and} \quad k \neq 0.
\]

Hence, the correct answer is $\boxed{D}$.

What is the fundamental difference between machine learning and statistics? In the Turing lecture 2010, Christopher Bishop mentions that machine learning is experiencing a revolution due to the application of statistics to its algorithms. However, this seems to suggest that all machine learning algorithms are essentially statistical algorithms. So, what sets these two disciplines apart? Why are they usually taught as separate courses in most universities?

The fields of Machine Learning (ML) and Statistics have a lot of overlap, but they are not exactly the same.

Statistics is a branch of mathematics that deals with the collection, analysis, interpretation, presentation, and organization of data. It provides tools for designing experiments and making inferences from data subject to randomness, with the aim of predicting general trends. It is more focused on the mathematical theory.

Machine Learning, on the other hand, is a subfield of artificial intelligence that focuses on the development of algorithms and statistical models that computer systems use to perform tasks without explicit instructions. While it does use statistical techniques, the goal is more on the practical application and usage of these models to allow machines to learn from and make decisions or predictions based on data. 

The distinction often comes from the goal of the user. A statistician is interested in inference, that is, understanding the structure of the data and the relationships between different variables. They want to understand the process that generates the data. On the other hand, a machine learning practitioner is often more interested in prediction. They want to know what is likely to happen in the future, given the data that they have.

While there is a significant overlap, they are separate courses because they have different focuses and require different skill sets. A course in statistics will focus more on the theory and mathematical basis of the techniques, while a machine learning course will focus more on how to use and implement the algorithms in a practical setting.

```python
import numpy as np

def batch_and_pad(sequences, max_length):
    batch_size = len(sequences)
```

A Ferris wheel has a diameter of 50 meters and is located 20 meters above the ground. The wheel completes one rotation in 4 minutes. Determine the maximum height above the ground that a rider will reach on the Ferris wheel, and at what times during the rotation this height is reached.

The maximum height a rider will reach on the Ferris wheel can be found by adding the radius of the wheel to the distance it is above the ground. Since the diameter of the wheel is 50 meters, the radius is half of that, which is 25 meters. The wheel is located 20 meters above the ground, so the maximum height a rider will reach is:

Maximum height = Radius + Distance above ground
Maximum height = 25 meters + 20 meters
Maximum height = 45 meters

Now, we need to determine at what times during the rotation this height is reached. Since the wheel completes one rotation in 4 minutes, the rider will be at the maximum height when they are at the top of the wheel. This occurs twice during one rotation: once when the rider starts at the top and once when they complete the rotation and return to the top.

To find the time it takes for the rider to reach the maximum height for the first time, we can simply divide the rotation time by 2:

Time to reach maximum height (first time) = Rotation time / 2
Time to reach maximum height (first time) = 4 minutes / 2
Time to reach maximum height (first time) = 2 minutes

The rider will reach the maximum height for the second time when they complete the rotation and return to the top:

Time to reach maximum height (second time) = Rotation time
Time to reach maximum height (second time) = 4 minutes

So, a rider will reach the maximum height of 45 meters above the ground at 2 minutes and 4 minutes during the rotation.

```python
def get_type_hierarchy(obj):
```

what is the value of

suggesting that \( z \) could be \( \text{cis}{\frac{\pi}{4}} \) or \( \text{cis}{-\frac{\pi}{4}} \).

Hence,

\]

- For a number to have more $1$'s than $0$'s in base-2, it must satisfy $k+1 > \frac{d+1}{2} \Longrightarrow k \ge \frac{d}{2}$. We sum the counts of such numbers from rows $0$ to $9$.

Conclusion:
$$ M \mod 500 = 561 \mod 500 = \boxed{61} $$

In an extended Morse code system, each symbol is represented by a sequence of dashes and dots. How many distinct symbols can be represented using sequences of 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 total dots and/or dashes, where sequences with 2 or more dashes must contain an even number of dashes?

Let's analyze each case:

**Case I: 1 dot or dash**
- Two possibilities: one dot, or one dash.

**Case II: 2 dots or dashes**
- Each symbol must contain an even number of dashes. Thus, the possibilities are two dots, or two dashes: 2 possibilities.

**Case III: 3 dots or dashes**
- Each symbol can contain 0, 1, or 3 dashes, but only sequences with 0 dashes (all dots) fulfill the even dash condition: 1 possibility.

**Case IV: 4 dots or dashes**
- Each symbol containing an even number of dashes: zero dashes (all dots), two dashes, or four dashes.
  - Zero dashes: 1 possibility.
  - Two dashes: $2^2 = 4$ arrangements of two dashes and two dots.
  - Four dashes: 1 possibility.
  - Total for 4 dots/dashes: $1 + 4 + 1 = 6$ possibilities.

**Case V: 5 dots or dashes**

  - Zero dashes (all dots): 1 possibility.
  - Two dashes: $2^3 = 8$ arrangements of two dashes and three dots.
  - Total for 5 dots/dashes: $1 + 8 = 9$ possibilities.

Adding them up, the total number of sequences is $2 + 2 + 1 + 6 + 9 = \boxed{20}$ distinct symbols.

3. Calculate the difference between the current timestamp and the file's creation timestamp using `datetime.timedelta()`.
4. Return the result as a `timedelta` object.

Here is how you could implement such a function:

```python
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def get_file_lifetime(path: str, timestamp: datetime) -> timedelta:

        raise FileNotFoundError(f"File not found at path: {path}")

    lifetime = timestamp - file_creation_timestamp
    return lifetime
```

I am using the built-in Python ElementTree module and it's quite easy for me to access child nodes. However, I am facing difficulty in accessing parent or sibling nodes. Is there any way to do this efficiently without having to traverse through the entire tree?

```python
def get_parent_map(tree):
    parent_map = {c: p for p in tree.iter() for c in p}
    return parent_map
```

```python
parent_map = get_parent_map(tree)

```

When it comes to getting siblings, it's a bit more complex. Siblings are basically other children that have the same parent. So once you have the parent, you can iterate over its children:

```python
def get_siblings(el, parent_map):
    parent = parent_map.get(el)
    return [child for child in parent if child != el]
```

Let $\left\{a_{n}\right\}$ be a sequence of positive terms with the first term being 1, and satisfying the recurrence relation $(n+1) a_{n+1}^{2} - n a_{n}^{2} + a_{n} a_{n+1} = 0$ for $n=1, 2, 3, \ldots$. Find the general term $a_{n}$.

We start by analyzing the given recurrence relation and deriving the general term $\{a_n\}$.

Given:
$$(n+1) a_{n+1}^{2} - n a_{n}^{2} + a_{n} a_{n+1} = 0 \quad \text{for} \quad n=1,2,3,\cdots$$

#### Step 1: Simplify the provided recurrence relation
First, notice that the given recurrence relation can be restructured for simplification:
\[
(n+1) a_{n+1}^{2} - n a_{n}^{2} + a_{n} a_{n+1} = 0
\]
Rearrange this equation to help identify a recursive pattern:
\[
(n+1) a_{n+1}^{2} + a_n a_{n+1} = n a_n^2
\]
Factor the equation as:
\[
[(n+1) a_{n+1} - a_n] [ a_{n+1} + a_n] = 0
\]

#### Step 2: Consider possible cases for the factored terms
There are two cases to consider:
1. $(n+1) a_{n+1} - a_n = 0$
2. $a_{n+1} + a_n = 0$

Given $a_n > 0$, the term $a_{n+1} + a_n > 0$. Hence, the second case does not apply.

So, we use the first case:
\[
(n+1) a_{n+1} - a_n = 0
\]

#### Step 3: Solve the simplified recurrence relation
Now solve for $a_{n+1}$:
\[
(n+1) a_{n+1} = a_n
\]
\[
a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n}{n+1}
\]

#### Step 4: Derive the general solution
Using the recursive formula, we can express $a_{n+1}$ in terms of previous terms:
\[
a_2 = \frac{a_1}{2}
\]
\[
a_3 = \frac{a_2}{3} = \frac{a_1}{2 \cdot 3}
\]
Continuing this pattern:
\[
a_n = \frac{a_1}{n!}
\]

Given $a_1 = 1$ (the first term):
\[
a_n = \frac{1}{n}
\]

#### Conclusion:
The general term for the sequence $\{a_n\}$ is:
\[
\boxed{\frac{1}{n}}
\]

- The `functions` argument is a list of functions that should be applied sequentially to the input.
- The `predicate_check` argument is a function that takes the output of the previous function and determines if the pipeline should continue or stop.
- The `pipeline` function should apply each function in the `functions` list sequentially to the input.
- The pipeline should stop when the `predicate_check` function returns `True`.
- The `pipeline` function should return the final output.

Here's how you can implement the `pipeline` function:

```python
def pipeline(input, functions, predicate_check):
    output = input
    for func in functions:
        output = func(output)
        if predicate_check(output):
            break
    return output
```

All sides of the convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ are of equal length, and $\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = 90^\circ$.  What is the degree measure of $\angle F$?

With $AB = BC = CD = DE = EF = FA$ and $\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = 90^\circ$, the figure can be visualized as having a three-quadrant (effectively three-fourth of a square) structure from $A$ to $D$, forming a right-angled zigzag pattern from $A$ to $D$. The remaining portion from $D$ to $A$ needs to accommodate 270 degrees of internal angles (90 degrees each at $A$, $B$, and $C$). The total internal angles of a hexagon are $(6-2) \times 180^\circ = 720^\circ$. Up to vertex $D$, we have used $270^\circ$.

$E$ and $F$ will then complete the hexagon with $\angle D = \angle E = \angle F$. Let's denote these angles as $\theta$. So, $3\theta = 720^\circ - 270^\circ = 450^\circ$.

Thus, $\theta = \frac{450^\circ}{3} = 150^\circ$.

This implies $\angle F = 150^\circ$ since the symmetry of the hexagon from $D$ to $F$ will distribute the angles equally among $D$, $E$, and $F$. 

Therefore, the degree measure of $\angle F$ is $\boxed{150^\circ}$.

I am looking to process a set of .csv files using SQL queries in a scripting language such as Python or Ruby. Yes, it is indeed possible to perform SQL-like queries on a CSV file without having to run a database server. Both Python and Ruby have libraries that can facilitate this.

For Python, you can use the built-in `csv` module to handle CSV files and `sqlite3` module for in-memory SQL querying. 

Here is a sample code snippet:

```python
import csv
import sqlite3

# read the csv file
with open('your_file.csv', 'r') as f:
    dr = csv.DictReader(f) 
    to_db = [(i['col1'], i['col2']) for i in dr]

# create an in-memory SQLite database
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
cur = con.cursor()

# create a table and insert the csv data
cur.execute("CREATE TABLE t (col1, col2);")
cur.executemany("INSERT INTO t (col1, col2) VALUES (?, ?);", to_db)
con.commit()

# now you can run SQL queries on the 't' table
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE col1 = 'value';")
print(cur.fetchall())
```

For Ruby, the 'csv' and 'sequel' gems can be used:

```ruby
  Float :price
end

  items.insert(name: row['name'], price: row['price'].to_f)
end

```

Suppose \( z \) and \( w \) are complex numbers such that:
\[ |z| = |w| = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad z \overline{w} + \overline{z} w = 2. \]
Additionally, \( z \) and \( w \) are equidistant from a complex number \( u = x + yi \), meaning \( |z-u| = |w-u| \).
Find the largest possible value of the real part of \( z + w \).

Let \( z = a + bi \) and \( w = c + di \), and \( u = x + yi \). Given \( |z| = 1 \) and \( |w| = 1 \), we have:
\[ a^2 + b^2 = 1 \quad \text{and} \quad c^2 + d^2 = 1. \]
From \( z \overline{w} + \overline{z} w = 2 \):
\[ (a + bi)(c - di) + (a - bi)(c + di) = 2 \Rightarrow 2ac + 2bd = 2. \]
This simplifies to \( ac + bd = 1 \).

Additionally, \( |z-u| = |w-u| \) implies:
\[ (a-x)^2 + (b-y)^2 = (c-x)^2 + (d-y)^2. \]

Now, consider the real part of \( z + w \), \( a + c \):
\[ (a + c)^2 + (b + d)^2 = a^2 + 2ac + c^2 + b^2 + 2bd + d^2 = 2 + 2 = 4. \]
Thus,
\[ (a + c)^2 = 4 - (b + d)^2. \]
Maximizing \( a + c \) when \( (b + d)^2 \) is minimal. The minimum value for \( (b + d)^2 \) is 0, happening when \( b = -d \). Hence,
\[ (a + c)^2 = 4 \Rightarrow a + c = 2 \quad \text{or} \quad -2. \]
However, \( a + c = -2 \) implies \( a, c < 0 \) not fitting our maximum condition. So, we keep \( a + c = 2 \).

Conclusion:
\[ \text{The largest possible value of the real part of } z + w \text{ is } \boxed{2}. \]

Let $q$ be the probability that, in the process of repeatedly flipping a fair coin, one will encounter a run of $6$ heads before one encounters a run of $2$ tails. Given that $q$ can be written in the form $m/n$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers, find $m+n$.

We model the process by using a state approach:
- State $H^k$ represents a sequence ending in exactly $k$ heads and not more, for $1 \leq k \leq 5$.
- State $T$ means any sequence ending in a single T (resetting the head count).

The transition probabilities based on the fairness of the coin (each coin flip resulting in heads or tails with probability $1/2$) are:
- From state $H^k$ to $H^{k+1}$ with probability $1/2$, for $1 \leq k \leq 4$.
- From every state $H^k$ to state $T$ with probability $1/2$.
- From state $T$ to $H^1$ with probability $1/2$, and staying in state $T$ with probability $1/2$.

The winning condition starts from any state $H^k$ and goes consecutively to $H^6$ without hitting state $T$ twice.

The probability of transitioning from $T$ to $H^1$ and successively going to $H^6$ can be described as:
- Start at $H^1$, proceed to $H^6$ with probability $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6 = \frac{1}{64}$.

The probability of doing this starting at $T$ simplifies as an infinite series where each term represents success starting after n times going back to $T$. Hence, the total probability $q$ can be expressed as $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \left(\frac{15}{32}\right)^n \left(\frac{1}{64}\right)$ by extension of the state reaching $H^6$.
This results in a geometric series $\frac{1}{128} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - \frac{15}{32}} = \frac{1}{128} \cdot \frac{32}{17} = \frac{2}{17}$.

Thus, $q = \frac{2}{17}$, and hence, $m+n = 2+17 = \boxed{19}$.

For example, given `s = "My name is {0}, I'm {1} years old."` and `v = ["Bob", "12"]`, the function should return `"My name is Bob, I'm 12 years old."`.

To solve this problem, we can use the `re` module to find all occurrences of `{n}` in the string `s`, and then substitute them with the n-th string in the list `v`.

Here's an implementation of the `format_string` function in Python:

```python
import re

def format_string(s, v):
    def replacer(match):
        index = int(match.group(1))
        return v[index] if index < len(v) else ''

    return re.sub(r'\{(\d+)\}', replacer, s)
```

(I) Calculate $a_1$, $a_2$, $a_3$, $a_4$, and from these results, conjecture the general term formula for $a_n$.

(II) Use mathematical induction to prove the conjecture from part (I).

(I) For $n = 1$, $a_1 = S_1 = 2 - a_1$, so $a_1 = 1$.

For $n = 2$, we have $a_1 + a_2 = S_2 = 4 - a_2$. Solving for $a_2$, we find $a_2 = \frac {3}{2}$.

Similarly, we find $a_3 = \frac {7}{4}$ and $a_4 = \frac {15}{8}$.

From this pattern, we conjecture that $a_n = \frac {2^n - 1}{2^{n-1}}$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}^*$.

(II) To prove this conjecture:
1. For $n = 1$, the left side is $a_1 = 1$, and the right side is also $1$. Therefore, the formula holds for $n = 1$.
2. Assume the formula holds for $n = k$ with $k \geq 1$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}^*$, meaning $a_k = \frac {2^k - 1}{2^{k-1}}$.
3. For $n = k + 1$, we have $a_{k+1} = S_{k+1} - S_k = 2(k + 1) - a_{k+1} - (2k - a_k) = 2 + a_k - a_{k+1}$.

5. This shows the formula also holds for $n = k + 1$.

By steps 1 and 2, the conjecture $a_n = \frac {2^n - 1}{2^{n-1}}$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}^*$.

\boxed{a_n = \frac {2^n - 1}{2^{n-1}}}

Given an array of integers and a target integer, write a Python function to calculate the number of subarrays that have a sum equal to the target.

The function should process the array in a single iteration, without extra memory usage.

Hints:
- Use a sliding window to process the array, where the window will slide over the array, starting from the first index.
- If the sum of the window is less than the target, add the right index, otherwise, subtract the left index.
- If the sum of the window equals the target, increment the count and add the right index.
- If the sum of the window is greater than the target, subtract the left index.
- If the left index is greater than or equal to the right index, reset both to 0, otherwise, keep sliding the window.

Your code should pass the following assertion:
```python

```

Here is a Python function that implements this approach:

```python
from typing import List

def subarray_sum(nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
    """
    Calculates the number of subarrays that have a sum equal to the target.
    """
    count = 0
    left = 0
    window_sum = 0

    for right, num in enumerate(nums):
        window_sum += num

        while left <= right and window_sum > target:
            window_sum -= nums[left]
            left += 1

        if window_sum == target:
            count += 1

    return count
```

This implementation uses a sliding window approach to process the array in a single iteration, without extra memory usage. The sliding window will slide over the array, starting from the first index. The `left` and `right` variables represent the left and right boundaries of the window, respectively. The `window_sum` variable represents the sum of the numbers in the window.

The `for` loop iterates over the `nums` array. The `window_sum` variable is updated with the current number from the array. The `while` loop checks if the sum of the window is greater than the target. If so, the left index is incremented and the corresponding number is removed from the window. This process is repeated until the sum of the window is less than or equal to the target.

If the sum of the window equals the target, the count is incremented and the right index is incremented. This process is repeated until the end of the array is reached.

To write a function to extract the data information, you can use Python's built-in `dir` function to retrieve the names of all attributes and `getattr` to access their values. We can then iterate over the attributes and apply the transformation function to each value.

1. **Setup and Induced Maps:**
   Let \( G \) be a hyper elementary abelian \( p \)-group and let \( f: G \rightarrow G \) be a homomorphism. We start with the short exact sequence (SES):
   \[
   0 \to C \to G \to P \to 0
   \]
   where \( C \) is cyclic of order relatively prime to that of \( P \) (i.e., \(\gcd(|P|, |C|) = 1\)). The map \( f \) induces maps \( f|_C: C \to C \), \( f: G \to G \), and \(\bar{f}: P \to P \).

2. **Application of the Snake Lemma:**
   By the Snake Lemma, we obtain the following exact sequence:
   \[
   0 \to \ker f|_C \to \ker f \to \ker \bar{f} \to \text{coker} f|_C \to \text{coker} f \to \text{coker} \bar{f} \to 0
   \]
   The connecting morphism \(\ker \bar{f} \to \text{coker} f|_C\) is the zero map due to the gcd condition, leading to two short exact sequences:
   \[
   0 \to \ker f|_C \to \ker f \to \ker \bar{f} \to 0
   \]
   and
   \[
   0 \to \text{coker} f|_C \to \text{coker} f \to \text{coker} \bar{f} \to 0
   \]

3. **Splitting of Short Exact Sequences:**
   By applying \(\text{Ext}^{*}(P, -)\) and considering the gcd condition, we see that the SESs are split. This means:
   \[
   \ker f \cong \ker f|_C \oplus \ker \bar{f}
   \]
   and
   \[
   \text{coker} f \cong \text{coker} f|_C \oplus \text{coker} \bar{f}
   \]

4. **Isomorphism of Kernels and Cokernels:**
   Since \( C \) and \( P \) are cyclic and the orders of all the kernels and cokernels are the same, we have:
   \[
   \ker f|_C \cong \text{coker} f|_C
   \]
   and
   \[
   \ker \bar{f} \cong \text{coker} \bar{f}
   \]

5. **Conclusion:**
   Combining the isomorphisms, we get:
   \[
   \ker f \cong \ker f|_C \oplus \ker \bar{f} \cong \text{coker} f|_C \oplus \text{coker} \bar{f} \cong \text{coker} f
   \]

The sum of the first n terms of the sequence $a_n$ is $S_n$, and $S_n = 3^n - 2$ where $n$ belongs to the positive natural numbers. Find the general term $a_n$.

Given that the sum of the first n terms of the sequence $\{a_n\}$ is $S_n$ and $S_n = 3^n - 2$ for $n$ belonging to the positive natural numbers,

First, we find the first term as follows:
\[a_1 = S_1 = 3^1 - 2 = 1.\]

Next, we find $a_n$ by subtracting the sum of the first $n-1$ terms from the sum of the first $n$ terms:
\[a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} = (3^n - 2) - (3^{n-1} - 2).\]

Now let us simplify the right side:
\begin{align*}
a_n &= (3^n - 2) - (3^{n-1} - 2) \\
&= 3^n - 3^{n-1} \\
&= 3^{n-1} \cdot (3 - 1) \\
&= 2 \cdot 3^{n-1}.
\end{align*}

Therefore, we reach the following piecewise definition based on the initial term:
\[a_n = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{for } n=1, \\
2 \cdot 3^{n-1} & \text{for } n \geq 2.
\end{cases}\]

To summarize the full solution:
\[a_n = \boxed{\begin{cases}
1 & \text{for } n=1, \\
2 \cdot 3^{n-1} & \text{for } n \geq 2.
\end{cases}}\]

In this problem, we apply the fundamental formula for finding the general term of a sequence by considering the sum of the sequence's first n terms. This is a foundational problem that requires careful interpretation of the problem statement and applying the formula for the nth term flexibly.

Write a Python function that takes a list of strings `strings` and a list of integers `lengths` as inputs, and returns a list of tuples `(string, length)` where `string` is the element from `strings` and `length` is the element from `lengths`.

For example, given `strings = ['a', 'b', 'c']` and `lengths = [1, 2, 3]`, the function should return `[(a, 1), (b, 2), (c, 3)]`.

Here's an example implementation of the function:

```python
def zip_strings_and_lengths(strings, lengths):
    if len(strings) != len(lengths):
        return []
    tuples = []
    for i in range(len(strings)):
        string = strings[i]
        length = lengths[i]
        tuples.append((string, length))

    return tuples
```

This implementation checks if the lengths of the two lists are the same before proceeding. If they are not equal, it returns an empty list. Otherwise, it loops over the `strings` list, creating a tuple for each element using the corresponding length from the `lengths` list and appending it to the list of tuples.

ABC is a triangle. A circle through A and B meets the sides AC, BC at D, E respectively. The lines AB and DE meet at F. The lines BD and CF meet at M. Show that M is the midpoint of CF if and only if \( MB \cdot MD = MC^2 \).

#### Objective:
We need to show that point \( M \) is the midpoint of \( CF \) if and only if \( MB \cdot MD = MC^2 \).

#### Step-by-Step Solution:

1. **Given Condition:**
   Assume that \( MB \cdot MD = MC^2 \).

2. **Proportionality and Similar Triangles:**
   We can rewrite this condition using proportions:
   \[
   MB \cdot MD = MC^2 \implies \frac{MB}{MC} = \frac{MC}{MD}
   \]
   This implies that:
   \[
   \triangle CMD \sim \triangle BMC
   \]
   by the definition of similar triangles (since corresponding sides are in proportion).

3. **Angle Relationships:**
   From the similarity, we know that:
   \[
   \angle MCD = \angle MBC
   \]

4. **Cyclic Quadrilateral Property:**
   Notice that points \( A \), \( B \), \( E \), and \( D \) lie on a circle. Because of this cyclic quadrilateral:
   \[
   \angle MBC = \angle DAE
   \]
   
5. **Parallel Lines Argument:**
   Therefore, we have \( \angle MCD = \angle DAE \). This angle equality shows that line \( AE \) is parallel to line \( CF \).

6. **Reverse Argument:**
   To show the converse, assume that the midpoint condition holds, i.e., \( M \) is the midpoint of \( CF \). Let us recall Ceva's theorem on triangle \( BCF \) with cevians \( BD \), \( CF \), and \( AE \) intersecting at point \( F \):
   \[
   \left(\frac{BA}{AF}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{CE}{EB}\right) \cdot 1 = 1
   \]
   
7. **Equal Ratios:**
   From Ceva's theorem and the fact \( M \) is the midpoint (hence \( AE \parallel CF \)):
   \[
   \frac{BA}{AF} = \frac{BE}{EC}
   \]

8. **Using Parallel Lines:**
   Since \( AE \parallel CF \), we deduce that \( MB \cdot MD = MC^2 \) by similar triangles argument mirrored.

#### Conclusion:
We have proved both directions of the if-and-only-if statement by using properties of similar triangles, cyclic quadrilaterals, and Ceva's Theorem combined with the given condition.

\[ \boxed{MB \cdot MD = MC^2} \]

two trains of equal lengths take 10 sec and 15 sec , respectively , to cross a telegraph post . if the length of each train is 120 m , in what time will they cross each other , travelling in opposite directions ?

Let's denote the speed of the first train as \( V_1 \) and the speed of the second train as \( V_2 \).

Since both trains take different times to cross a telegraph post, we can calculate their speeds using the formula:

\[ \text{Speed} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}} \]

For the first train:
\[ V_1 = \frac{\text{Length of the train}}{\text{Time taken to cross the post}} \]
\[ V_1 = \frac{120 \text{ m}}{10 \text{ sec}} \]
\[ V_1 = 12 \text{ m/sec} \]

For the second train:
\[ V_2 = \frac{\text{Length of the train}}{\text{Time taken to cross the post}} \]
\[ V_2 = \frac{120 \text{ m}}{15 \text{ sec}} \]
\[ V_2 = 8 \text{ m/sec} \]

When two trains are moving in opposite directions, their relative speed is the sum of their individual speeds. Therefore, the relative speed \( V_{\text{relative}} \) is:

\[ V_{\text{relative}} = V_1 + V_2 \]
\[ V_{\text{relative}} = 12 \text{ m/sec} + 8 \text{ m/sec} \]
\[ V_{\text{relative}} = 20 \text{ m/sec} \]

When the two trains cross each other, the distance covered is the sum of their lengths, since both are of equal length, the total distance \( D \) is:

\[ D = \text{Length of first train} + \text{Length of second train} \]
\[ D = 120 \text{ m} + 120 \text{ m} \]
\[ D = 240 \text{ m} \]

Now, we can find the time \( T \) it takes for them to cross each other using the formula:

\[ \text{Time} = \frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Speed}} \]

\[ T = \frac{D}{V_{\text{relative}}} \]
\[ T = \frac{240 \text{ m}}{20 \text{ m/sec}} \]
\[ T = 12 \text{ sec} \]

So, the two trains will cross each other in $\boxed{12}$  seconds when travelling in opposite directions.

Polymorphism in the Angiotensinogen Gene, Hypertension, and Ethnic Differences in the Risk of Recurrent Coronary Events
Ilan Goldenberg, Arthur J. Moss, Daniel Ryan, Scott McNitt, Shirley W. Eberly, Wojciech Zareba
https://doi.org/10.1161/01.HYP.0000239204.41079.6b
Arthur J. Moss
Scott McNitt
Shirley W. Eberly
The M235T mutation of the human angiotensinogen gene has been shown to be associated with elevated circulating angiotensinogen concentrations and essential hypertension. The frequencies of the 235T allele are significantly different in black and white subjects. We analyzed the independent contribution of the angiotensinogen M235T mutation to the development of recurrent coronary events (coronary-related death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unstable angina) in a cohort of 916 black (n=145) and white (n=771) postmyocardial infarction patients who were prospectively studied during an average follow-up of 28 months. The frequency of the 235T allele was significantly higher among black (82%) than among white (44%) patients (P<0.001). There was no evidence for Hardy–Weinberg disequilibrium. During follow-up, 41 cardiac events (28%) occurred in blacks and 197 (26%) in whites (P=0.49). Multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression analysis demonstrated that 235T homozygosity was independently associated with increased risk of coronary events among black (hazard ratio: 2.37; P=0.04) but not white (hazard ratio: 0.93; P=0.68) patients, with a significant ethnic-related interaction effect (P for the difference=0.04). Among hypertensive black patients, the TT genotype was associated with a 3.3-fold (P=0.02) increase in the risk of coronary events. Our findings suggest that homozygosity for the 235T mutation in the angiotensinogen gene is an independent risk factor for coronary events in black postmyocardial infarction patients. The presence of hypertension significantly augments the risk associated with this genetic mutation.
Coronary heart disease (CHD) is a multifactorial condition influenced by environmental and genetic factors. The renin–angiotensin system plays an important role in cardiovascular physiology. Angiotensin II may have direct toxic effects on myocardial cells, activates the sympathetic nervous system, stimulates fibroblast proliferation, and vasoconstricts coronary vessels.1,2 Angiotensinogen (AGT) is major precursor of this system, and its plasma levels have been shown to correlate with blood pressure.3,4 The human AGT gene has been identified.5,6 The T allele of a polymorphism, which encodes threonine instead of methionine at position 235 (M235T), has been shown to be associated with increased circulating AGT concentrations7 and an increased risk of essential hypertension.7–10 Apart from hypertension, which is a well-established risk factor for CHD, several studies have reported a significant association with the risk of CHD or myocardial infarction (MI) among individuals with the TT genotype.11–13 However, a recent meta-analysis failed to detect such an association.14 Notably, published data are limited mostly to white and Asian subjects, whereas the association between the AGT polymorphism and CHD among black subjects, in whom the average allele frequencies of 235T are significantly higher,14 has not been studied.
Available evidence suggests that the outcome of black patients after an acute coronary event is different than whites, with a higher case fatality rate among the former population reported in several studies.15,16 It is possible that variations in risk factors, including genotype and hypertension or its treatment, may also contribute to the different outcome of black and white patients.
We hypothesized that AGT 235T homozygosity may confer a different risk of recurrent coronary events in post-MI black and white subjects enrolled in the prospective Thrombogenic Factors and Coronary Events (THROMBO) Study. We also studied the independent contribution of the TT genotype to the risk of recurrent coronary events among hypertensive and nonhypertensive patients and the relationship between the benefit of therapy with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and the AGT M235T mutation.
The THROMBO Study was a prospective, multicenter investigation that enrolled patients with acute MI from 13 participating hospitals in the United States between October 1, 1994, and June 30, 1997. A total of 1161 patients were enrolled at the time of hospital discharge. Blood samples for genetic analysis were collected at study enrollment on 1012 of the enrolled patients. The average follow-up was 28 months. The details of this study have been reported in the primary publication, and the clinical parameters that defined this study population included a full spectrum of traditional postinfarction risk factors.17 The study was composed mainly of 3 self-reported ethnic populations: blacks (n=145), Latinos (n=81), and whites (n=771) living in the United States; other populations including Asian or Pacific Islanders, American Indians, native Alaskans, and Indians composed a relatively small proportion of study patients (n=15). In the current study, we compared the clinical course of black and white patients (n=916).
Demographic information and medical history were obtained on enrollment in the trial, and medication usage was recorded during the baseline visit 2 months after the index MI. Ejection fraction was determined by an echocardiogram, a nuclear study, or angiography during the initial hospitalization after the MI. Patients were categorized as having a history of hypertension if they were ever treated with antihypertensive medications before their index MI. A single blood pressure measurement was taken before discharge; however, blood pressure was not monitored throughout the study, because hypertension was not the primary scope of the original THROMBO Study.
The prespecified coronary event end points were first occurrence of death from CHD, enzyme-documented nonfatal MI, and hospitalization for unstable angina. A 2-member committee categorized the coronary events from appropriate medical records according to prespecified written criteria. The risk of the end point was assessed by ethnicity and stratified by the presence of the AGT M235T mutation (categorized in the primary analysis as TT genotype carriers versus MM or MT genotype carriers), hypertension, and treatment with ACE inhibitors.
Blood (55 mL) was drawn in the fasting state at the baseline clinic visit 2 months after the index MI. Plasma and serum samples were each separated, frozen, and sent to Rochester, NY, for central storage in a −70°C freezer. Colorimetric assays were used to measure total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides (all by Vitros Chemistry Products); apolipoprotein A-I and B were measured by Beckman Immunochemistry Systems; lipoprotein (a) was measured by immunoassay (Macra, Strategic Diagnostics); and insulin was measured by radioimmunoassay (Coat-A-Count Diagnostic Products). The concentration of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was calculated by the Friedewald formula.18 Analyses were run according to the manufacturers’ specifications, and quality control was within the recommended precision for each test.
Buffy coats were isolated and stored at −70°C until extracted for DNA analysis. Genotyping was performed through a contractual agreement with Millennium Pharmaceuticals. The AGT (M235T) polymorphism was typed using the TaqMan method. Primers used were: AGT1, 59 GAT GCG CAC AAG GTC CTG TC39 and AGT2, 59 CAG GGT GCT GTC CAC ACT GGC TCG C.8 TaqMan assays were validated by retesting 5% to 10% of samples using independent methods, including melting curve analysis (Light Cycler, Roche Diagnostics) or PCR/restriction digest. If >1% disagreement was present between assays, PCR/restriction digest was used as a definitive standard to determine the correct assignment of the discrepant samples, and all 1012 of the samples were reassayed using the validated methods.
The clinical characteristics and genotype frequencies of black and white patients were compared using the χ2 test and the Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. The Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (which predicts genotype frequencies in populations) was tested in both ethnic groups.19 The Kaplan–Meier life table method was used to assess the time to first coronary end point and the cumulative event rates for each group and within each group by genotype and hypertension. The results were compared using the log-rank test.
The outcome analysis used the Cox proportional hazards survivorship model. The outcome measure was time from enrollment to a first recurrent coronary event. In the analysis of the effect of medical therapy on outcome, follow-up was assessed from the baseline 2-month visit. A stepwise forward selection procedure was used to identify important clinical risk predictors for the time to end point. Ethnicity, hypertension, and the additional contribution of the AGT M235T mutation to the basic clinical model were forced into the model. Analyses were performed with the use of SAS software (version 9.13). A 2-sided P<0.05 was used for declaring statistical significance.
The clinical characteristics, medical therapy, and laboratory of study patients by ethnic group are presented in Table 1A. Compared with black patients, white patients were older, had a higher proportion of males, and a lower body mass index; the proportion of patients with hypertension and diabetes mellitus was significantly higher among black patients. Predischarge systolic and diastolic blood pressures were significantly higher among black than white patients. In patients with a history of hypertension, mean systolic blood pressure was 10 mm Hg higher than those without a history of hypertension (124 versus 114 mm Hg; P<0.001), whereas diastolic blood pressure was 3 mm Hg higher among hypertensive patients (72 versus 69 mm Hg; P=0.01). During follow-up, medical therapy with ACE inhibitors, calcium-channel blockers, and nitrates was administered more frequently to black as compared with white patients. Thrombolytic therapy during the index MI and revascularization procedures during follow-up were administered to a similar proportion of black and white patients. The 2 ethnic groups displayed similar serum levels of total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol but significantly different levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides.

Effect of AGT M235T Polymorphism on the Risk of Recurrent Coronary Events in Black and White Patients
During an average follow-up of 28 months, 238 patients experienced a first recurrent coronary event, including 41 black patients (28%) and 197 white patients (26%; P=0.49). The presence of 235T homozygosity was independently associated with a significant increase in the risk of recurrent coronary events among black patients but not among white patients (P value for TT genotype×ethnic interaction=0.04; Table 3). Among the former ethnic group, there was a significant 2.4-fold increase in the risk of coronary events in patients carrying the genotype, which was attributed mainly to the presence of the TT genotype in hypertensive patients (3.3-fold increase; P=0.02).

At 2 years, the probability of a first recurrent coronary event was 32% among black patients with the TT genotype as compared with 16% among patients with either the MM or MT genotypes (Figure 1A), whereas the probability of recurrent coronary events was similar among white patients with and without the TT genotype (Figure 1B). The significant increase in the rate of recurrent coronary events among blacks with the TT genotype was observed mainly in hypertensive patients (2-year rates for TT genotype versus MM or MT carriers: 40% and 14%, respectively; P=0.015; data not shown), whereas among nonhypertensive blacks, event rates were identical (16%) in TT and non-TT genotype carriers (data not shown).

Relation of the AGT M235T Mutation to Ethnic Differences in the Risk of Recurrent Coronary Events
The adjusted risk of recurrent coronary events was similar among black patients and white patients (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.09; 95% CI: 0.75 to 1.60; P=0.66). However, when stratified by the presence of hypertension or the TT genotype, the risk of events was higher in black than white patients with either risk factor (Table 4). Furthermore, among patients with a combination of the 2 risk factors, there was a >2-fold increase in the risk of recurrent coronary events among black as compared with white patients. By contrast, no significant differences in the risk between the 2 groups were detected among nonhypertensive patients and non-TT genotype carriers (P for interaction between high-risk and low-risk groups=0.02). Accordingly, Kaplan–Meier curves, describing the probability of a first coronary event, demonstrated similar rates among black and white patients (Figure 2, a marginally significant difference between the 2 ethnic groups among hypertensive patients (Figure 2B), and a significantly higher rate of events among hypertensive blacks with the TT genotype (Figure 2C).

Relation of AGT M235T Mutation to Benefit of Therapy With ACE Inhibitors
Baseline medical therapy with ACE inhibitors was associated with a marginally significant 23% reduction in the risk of recurrent coronary events in study patients (P=0.11). Risk reduction with ACE inhibitor therapy was nonsignificantly higher in blacks as compared with white patients (41% versus 19%, respectively; P for ACE inhibitor×ethnic interaction=0.45).
When stratified by the presence of the M235T mutation, the benefit of ACE inhibitor therapy was more pronounced among patients identified as homozygous carriers of the 235T allele (adjusted HR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.27 to 1.04; P=0.06) than among MM or MT genotype carriers (adjusted HR: 0.89; 95% CI: 0.60 to 1.32; P=0.56).
In this prospective study of post-MI patients, we have shown that the AGT M235T mutation confers a different risk of recurrent coronary events in black and white patients. Blacks, identified as homozygous carriers of the AGT 235T allele, had a significantly higher risk of coronary events during follow-up as compared with non-TT carriers. The positive correlation between genotype and coronary risk in this population was observed mainly among hypertensive patients. By contrast, no significant association between the AGT M235T mutation and outcome was shown in hypertensive and nonhypertensive whites.
A higher rate of adverse events after MI among black patients as compared with white patients was reported previously and was ascribed to differences in blood pressure control, access to health care, socioeconomic status, and risk factor management.15,16,20–22 In addition, a higher prevalence of hypertension in black than white patients has been suggested to contribute to the different risk for CHD and outcome.16,21 In the current study, we have shown that the higher risk of recurrent coronary events among hypertensive blacks as compared with whites was attributed mainly to subjects identified as TT-genotype carriers. Notably, the increase in the risk in the former ethnic group occurred despite similar rates of early intervention during the index MI and revascularization procedures during follow-up.
In a recent meta-analysis of 45 267 subjects, the TT genotype was shown to be associated with a 19% and 60% increase in risk of hypertension in white and Asian individuals, respectively, whereas no association with the risk of CHD or MI was detected in these 2 populations.14 These data are in agreement with a previous report on white and Asian subjects.23 The present study is the first to analyze the association between the AGT M235T mutation and the risk of recurrent coronary events in post-MI patients. Consistent with these reports, we did not show a significant association between 235T homozygosity and the risk of coronary events in white patients. However, among black patients, in whom the relation between the M235T mutation and CHD risk was not studied previously, we have shown that the TT genotype is an independent risk factor, mainly in hypertensive patients.
Possible Explanation of the Association
Plasma renin activity (PRA) has been suggested as mechanism relating the AGT M235T mutation to adverse outcome in hypertensive patients.24 High PRA levels were shown to be significantly associated with increased risk of coronary events among hypertensive subjects,25 whereas a similar association was not demonstrated for normotensive subjects.26 The TT genotype was shown to be associated with a significant 11% increase in plasma AGT levels,14 and, under basal condition, carriers of this genotype were demonstrated to have lower PRA than MM or MT carriers.24 Therefore, it seems that higher AGT levels, associated with the TT genotype, lead to lower PRA levels in nonhypertensive patients. This is consistent with the known low-renin profiles in women and blacks.27 The frequency of the T allele was reported to be 81% in blacks,28 and women have also higher AGT levels because of the estrogen effect.29 However, patients carrying the TT genotype also have a higher potential to produce angiotensin II than non-TT carriers because of a higher availability of the renin substrate. Hypertension has been shown to increase PRA levels.25,26 Therefore, a possible explanation for the significant association between the TT genotype and the risk of coronary events in hypertensive black patients may be that a concurrent existence of high AGT concentration, associated with the TT genotype, and a stimulated PRA, associated with hypertension, can induce a sustained vascular response, leading to a potentially long-term adverse outcome. By contrast, the association between high AGT levels with lower PRA levels in nonhypertensive black TT carriers may result in a neutral effect of this genotype on outcome in this population.
The lack of a significant association between the AGT M235T mutation and the risk of recurrent coronary events in both hypertensive and nonhypertensive white patients suggests that the mutation plays a less dominant role in this population and that other observed or unobserved background risk factors may be more closely associated with outcome in white post-MI patients. It is also possible that the long-term effects of the AGT M235T mutation on the level of hypertension are more pronounced in black than in white patients, leading to a more adverse outcome among hypertensive patients with the genetic mutation in the former ethnic group.
ACE Inhibitor Therapy and the AGT M235T Mutation
Previous studies have suggested that treatment with ACE inhibitors has reduced efficacy in blacks for the end point of heart failure and that vasodilator therapy may be more effective in this population.30,31 However, the results of vasodilator trials were inconsistent and did not show a statistically significant interaction between treatment and ethnicity. Furthermore, the drug was shown to be equally efficacious in blacks and in whites in reducing the incidence of the combined end point of death or development of a new onset of heart failure.30 Similarly, no interaction with ethnicity was observed for the relative benefit of ACE inhibitors in the Antihypertensive and Lipid-Lowering Treatment to Prevent Heart Attack Trial.32 We have consistently shown similar trends suggesting that ACE inhibitor therapy is effective in black patients. Furthermore, treatment with the drug in both ethnic groups was associated with a trend toward greater risk reduction among TT-genotype carriers than among MM or MT carriers. Thus, our preliminary findings suggest that this form of medical therapy may be important in the treatment of post-MI black patients in whom the frequency of the TT genotype is ≈70%. These data need to be validated in future studies.
Several limitations of this study should be considered. The present results provide evidence of the association between the M235T mutation and the risk of recurrent coronary events in post-MI black patients at the gene level but do not demonstrate the direct mechanism by which the mutation affects outcome. In addition, further evaluation is required to determine whether AGT M235T polymorphism mediates coronary risk directly or acts as a marker of other gene polymorphisms.
We cannot rule out a “survival-of-the-fittest” bias in our post-MI cohort. High-risk white patients with the TT genotype may have died during the index event, leading to a reduced effect of the genotype on the risk of recurrent events among survivors. Approximately 15% of patients die during their first MI.33 Thus, considering the relatively low frequency of the TT genotype among white patients (≈20%), the potential contribution of such selection effects to outcome in this population is relatively small.
Treatment with ACE inhibitors was not randomly assigned in study patients. In addition, the lack of a significant interaction among the effect of this mode of therapy, ethnicity, and genotype may be because of sample size limitations. Therefore, the interpretation of the results regarding the efficacy of ACE inhibitor therapy should be reserved, despite adjustments for important clinical covariates.
Our data provide evidence that the TT genotype is an important factor affecting outcome after MI in hypertensive black patients and seems to play a less dominant role in nonhypertensive black and white patients. These findings suggest that the risk associated with renin–angiotensin system genetic polymorphisms may be different among ethnic groups and stress the importance of identifying specific genetic risk factors within individual ethnic populations. The data regarding ACE inhibitor efficacy in black post-MI patients and the relationship to polymorphism in the AGT gene suggest important therapeutic implications and need to be further evaluated in prospective randomized trials.

Let \( \omega \) be a nonreal root of \( z^3 = 1 \). Let \( a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \) be real numbers such that
\[
\frac{1}{a_1 + \omega} + \frac{1}{a_2 + \omega} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_n + \omega} = 3 + 4i.
\]
Compute
\[
\frac{2a_1 - 2}{a_1^2 - a_1 + 1} + \frac{2a_2 - 2}{a_2^2 - a_2 + 1} + \dots + \frac{2a_n - 2}{a_n^2 - a_n + 1}.
\]

We know \( \omega \) is a nonreal root of \( z^3 = 1 \), which implies \( \omega^3 = 1 \) and thus \( \omega^3 - 1 = 0 \). This factors as \( (\omega - 1)(\omega^2 + \omega + 1) = 0 \). Since \( \omega \) is nonreal, \( \omega^2 + \omega + 1 = 0 \). Therefore, using the conjugate root, the equation simplifies to:

\( \frac{1}{a_1 + \overline{\omega}} + \frac{1}{a_2 + \overline{\omega}} + \dots + \frac{1}{a_n + \overline{\omega}} = 3 - 4i. \)

Summing the original and its conjugate:

\[
\sum_{k=1}^n \left( \frac{1}{a_k + \omega} + \frac{1}{a_k + \overline{\omega}} \right) = 3 + 4i + 3 - 4i = 6.
\]

From the simplification:

\[
\frac{1}{a + \omega} + \frac{1}{a + \overline{\omega}} = \frac{a + \omega + a + \overline{\omega}}{(a + \omega)(a + \overline{\omega})} = \frac{2a + \omega + \overline{\omega}}{a^2 + (\omega + \overline{\omega}) a + \omega \overline{\omega}} = \frac{2a - 1}{a^2 - a + 1}.
\]

We factor out 2 from \( 2(2a_k - 2) \), adapting to the modified problem, simplifying to \( (2a_k - 2) \).

So:

\[
\sum_{k = 1}^n \frac{2a_k - 2}{a_k^2 - a_k + 1} = 6,
\]

\[
\boxed{6}.
\]

Conclusion:
Since the simplification of given expressions in terms of conjugates through \( \omega \) and \( \overline{\omega} \) double the resultant calculation, and the problem's hypothesis remains consistent through computation, we find that the solution to the problem is \( \boxed{6} \).

Given that the base of a triangle is $\left(2x+1\right)cm$ long and the height is $\left(x-2\right)cm$, if both the base and height are increased by $5$ centimeters, how much does the area of the triangle increase? Also, find the increase in area when $x=3$.

To solve this problem, let's break it down step by step, following the given solution closely:

1. **Initial Area Calculation**:
   The initial area of the triangle is given by the formula $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$. Substituting the given base and height, we have:
   \[
   \text{Initial Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times (2x + 1) \times (x - 2)
   \]

2. **New Area Calculation**:
   After increasing both the base and the height by $5$ cm, the new dimensions become $(2x + 1 + 5)$ for the base and $(x - 2 + 5)$ for the height. Thus, the new area is:
   \[
   \text{New Area} = \frac{1}{2} \times (2x + 6) \times (x + 3)
   \]

3. **Increase in Area**:
   The increase in area is the difference between the new area and the initial area. Substituting the expressions for the initial and new areas, we get:
   \begin{align*}
   \text{Increase in Area} &= \frac{1}{2} \times (2x + 6) \times (x + 3) - \frac{1}{2} \times (2x + 1) \times (x - 2) \\
   &= \frac{1}{2} \times (2x^2 + 6x + 6x + 18) - \frac{1}{2} \times (2x^2 - 4x + x - 2) \\
   &= \frac{1}{2} \times (2x^2 + 12x + 18) - \frac{1}{2} \times (2x^2 - 3x - 2) \\
   &= \frac{1}{2} \times (15x + 20) \\
   &= \frac{15}{2}x + 10
   \end{align*}

4. **Finding the Increase in Area for $x=3$**:
   Substituting $x = 3$ into the expression for the increase in area, we find:
   \[
   \text{Increase in Area} = \frac{15}{2} \times 3 + 10 = 22.5 + 10 = 32.5 \, \text{cm}^2
   \]

Therefore, the increase in area when $x=3$ is $\boxed{32.5 \, \text{cm}^2}$.

Can you explain the difference between Python's generators and iterators? Could you also provide some examples illustrating when each case would be more suitable?

In Python, both iterators and generators are used to iterate over a collection of items. However, they serve this purpose in slightly different ways.

An iterator is an object that implements the iterator protocol (which requires the `__iter__()` and `__next__()` methods). Here's an example of creating an iterator:

```python
class MyIterator:
    def __init__(self, letters):
        self.letters = letters
        self.position = 0

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self):
        if self.position >= len(self.letters):
            raise StopIteration
        letter = self.letters[self.position]
        self.position += 1
        return letter

letters_iter = MyIterator('abc')
for letter in letters_iter:
    print(letter)
```

A generator, on the other hand, is a more straightforward way to create an iterator. It’s a function that uses the keyword `yield` to generate a sequence of results instead of returning a single value. Unlike a function, it remembers its state between calls. Here's an example of a generator:

```python
def my_generator():
    yield 'a'
    yield 'b'
    yield 'c'

letters_gen = my_generator()
for letter in letters_gen:
    print(letter)
```

In terms of when you would use each, it depends on your specific needs. Generators are often easier to write and more readable, but they can only be iterated over once. If you need to create an object that can be iterated over multiple times, you might need to use an iterator. However, in many cases, a generator will suffice and will be the more straightforward option.

Exact asymptotic characterisation of running time for
approximate gradient descent on random graphs

Matthieu Jonckheere1

Manuel Sáenz2

Introduction

The last decades saw an exponential increase in the sizes of data sets available on many fields. Many tools and algorithms for managing it have been recently developed. But they usually come with very difficult technical issues, as implementing optimisation routines over spaces of high dimension, which may be extremely computationally demanding. In this context, first-order methods for solving optimisation problems have become a cornerstone of machine learning and operation research.

One of the basic (but very common in practice) strategies for minimisation is the celebrated gradient descent. It works by sequentially updating the function parameters in the opposite direction of its gradient. This procedure can be shown to lead, under general assumptions, to a local minimum. Because of the computational cost or the impossibility of computing the true gradient with respect to large collections of parameters, variants of the gradient descent are commonly used in practice. One of such variants is the well-known stochastic gradient descent, in which the same procedure is replaced by computing a stochastic approximation (usually a sample) of the cost function and which has been successful in machine learning applications.

In order to deal with high-dimensionality and complexity, a lot of research has focused on iterative methods that, at each iteration, only optimise over a subset of the decision variables. In this framework, several procedures have been proposed: block-coordinate descent methods, which alternates the optimisation steps between blocks of selected variables (see also variations around the randomised Kaczmarz algorithm), or randomised block-coordinate and alternating randomised block coordinate descent. In this last version, the algorithm alternates gradient descents steps (or exact optimisation) on randomly selected blocks. Optimisation via sequential exploration is also relevant for many social, economic, and ecological data sets that are structured as graphs. A crucial task in those contexts is to find vertices that locally minimise/maximise some function over the underlying network. For instance, many problems have been modelled as potential games whose Nash equilibria are given by the maxima of a potential. These problems have motivated recent studies on optimisation of graph functions. For example, some algorithms were proposed to find extremes of graph functions efficiently, while in, the best response dynamics was studied as an algorithm to find Nash equilibria in random potential games.

In this work, we study a toy model based on random graphs to understand possible drastically different regimes concerning the behaviour of this type of strategies. We model the states of the optimisation problem by the nodes of a random network, where the edges correspond to possible explorations of a new state from a given state. The fact that randomisation/block coordinates procedures are used is reflected in the randomness of the adjacency matrix of the network.

We make two more modelling assumptions. First the value of the cost to be optimised will be given by a random field (on the nodes of the networks) and the mean number of states explored during the exploration scales according to the connectivity of the networks, which in turn is a function of the total number of nodes. This scaling is such that the total number of neighbours considered at each exploration step is of order $1$ (which makes sense in practice).

We focus here on the case of i.i.d values for the cost at each node which is of course an over-simplistic assumption. However, it has two main advantages: (i) it allows to perform a very detailed theoretical analysis, (ii) we believe that the obtained structural results might also be relevant for more general fields with sufficiently low correlations. More complex correlations structures will be considered in on-going work.

Contribution

We study in detail this simple model of sequential exploration on Erdös-Rényi graphs, giving first quantitative results for approximate gradient optimisation. We derive the running time complexity for the whole range of parametrisations of the connection probability, finding in each case its asymptotic behaviour. We further show that, in these structures, this algorithm is faster (in a stochastic order sense) than any other local search algorithm. In this way, these results provide a possible way of understanding the improvement in the performance achieved by stochastic variants of gradient descent. It also allows to give asymptotic estimates of the complexity of finding Nash equilibria in sparse random potential games as considered in.

The remaining of the paper is organised as follows. In Section 2 we present the main results of the chapter, how they relate to each other, and we discuss how they characterise the complexity of the algorithm. While in Section 3 we present a simplified dynamics that will be of key importance in deriving these results. And finally, in Section 4 we give the proofs for Erdös-Rényi graphs.

Description of the process studied

We focus on Erdös-Rényi graphs with $n$ nodes with connection probabilities $p$ that scale with respect to the graph size according to $p(n)= \lambda n^{-\alpha}$ (with $\lambda > 0$ and $0 < \alpha < 1$).

We present in Algorithms 1 and 2 respectively the pseudo-code for the Gradient Descent (GD) algorithm and for the local optimisation algorithm studied, which we will refer to as approximate gradient descent (AGD).
